sessions.topic: Leash training for a new dog

turns.text: Hi! I'm Nell. I just adopted a beagle named Biscuit and he pulls on the leash like crazy. Any tips?

Congratulations on Biscuit! Beagles are scent hounds, so the pulling is usually his nose leading the way. A few things that help:
1. Stop moving the moment the leash goes tight, and only walk on when it's slack.
2. Reward him for walking at your side with small, smelly treats.
3. Give him sniff breaks on cue, so he learns when it's his time to explore.
4. Keep early sessions short: ten minutes, a few times a day.
A front-clip harness can also take the edge off while he learns.
We walk along Cherry Creek here in Denver most mornings. It's busy with bikes. Should I avoid it?

Busy paths are hard at first. Try quieter side streets for the first week or two, then go back to Cherry Creek at off-peak times. When a bike passes, step to the side, ask for a sit, and give him a treat. He'll learn that bikes mean pause and get a snack.
Perfect, thank you!
You're welcome. Enjoy your walks with Biscuit!
Actually, one more question. What kind of treats work best for this, and how many is too many?

Small, soft and smelly is the rule for training treats. For a beagle, smell matters more than almost anything, so the stronger the better. Good options:
- Cooked chicken or turkey, cut into pea-sized pieces
- Small cubes of cheese (string cheese tears up easily)
- Commercial soft training treats, broken into smaller bits
- Freeze-dried liver, crumbled
- Plain cooked hot dog slices, used sparingly because they're salty

Size matters more than people expect. A treat should be about the size of a pea and gone in one quick chew. If he has to crunch for five seconds, he loses focus on the walk and you lose the rhythm of rewarding at the right moment.

A useful trick is to build a treat ladder:
1. Low value: his regular kibble. Use it indoors and in easy, quiet spots.
2. Medium value: commercial training treats. Use them on ordinary walks.
3. High value: real chicken or cheese. Save it for hard moments, like a bike passing or a squirrel darting across the path.

As for how many: a common guideline is to keep treats under about 10 percent of his daily calories. On heavy training days, just trim his meal portion a little to make up for it. You can also measure out part of his breakfast and use those pieces as rewards on the walk, so it adds nothing extra at all.

Carry them somewhere you can reach fast, like a treat pouch on your hip or a jacket pocket. The reward needs to land within a second or two of the behavior you want, or he won't connect the two.
Can you explain the front-clip harness more? How should it fit?

A front-clip harness has the leash ring on the chest instead of the back. When he pulls, the leash pressure turns his body gently to the side and back toward you, instead of letting him lean into it like a sled dog. It doesn't stop pulling by itself, but it takes away some of the payoff while you teach the real skill.

How it should fit:
1. The chest strap should sit across the breastbone, low enough that it doesn't press on his throat.
2. The strap behind the front legs should sit about a hand's width behind the elbows so it doesn't rub his armpits.
3. You should be able to slide two fingers under any strap, but not much more. Too loose and he can back out of it; too tight and it chafes.
4. The front ring should sit in the center of his chest, not off to one side.

Things to watch for:
- Rubbing or red patches under the front legs after a walk. That usually means it's sitting too far forward or is too snug.
- His gait. If his front legs look restricted or he's shortening his stride, try a different style. Y-shaped harnesses tend to leave the shoulders freer than the straight-across style.
- Escaping. Beagles can be surprisingly good at slipping out of things. Test it indoors by gently pulling backward on the leash; if it starts to slide over his head, tighten it.

Introduce it slowly. Let him sniff it, give a treat, put it on for a minute indoors with a few more treats, then take it off. Do that a few times before the first walk so it becomes a normal part of getting ready.

One more tip: some people use a double-ended leash that clips to both the front ring and a back ring. That gives you a bit more control, and you can use the back ring alone for relaxed sniff time.
What do I do when he stops dead to sniff something and won't budge?

That's classic beagle behavior. His nose is basically his main way of reading the world, so the goal isn't to stop sniffing. It's to make sniffing something you take turns on.

When he plants himself and won't budge:
1. Don't drag him. Pulling him away tends to make him dig in harder, and it teaches him the leash is a tug-of-war.
2. Wait a few seconds. Many dogs finish on their own if you just stand still and stay calm.
3. Use a cheerful cue like 'let's go' and take a step or two in the new direction, with light leash pressure that you release the instant he turns toward you.
4. If that doesn't work, lure him: put a treat right at his nose, lead him a few steps with it, then reward when he's walking with you again.

Then build a sniff cue so he has a clear on and off switch:
- At a good spot, say 'go sniff' and let him explore on a looser leash.
- After a short while, say 'let's go' and reward heavily when he comes along.
- Do this several times per walk. When he knows sniff breaks come regularly, he's less frantic about grabbing every smell he passes.

Practice 'let's go' indoors first, where there's nothing exciting. Say the cue, step backward, and give him a treat when he follows. Once that's easy, try it on a quiet street, then on busier stretches.

Also plan for some walks that are purely about sniffing. A slow ten-minute walk where he leads, within reason, tires him out mentally more than a fast long walk, and a tired beagle pulls less on the next outing.
Could you write out a simple two-week plan I can follow?

Here's a simple plan. Keep each session short and end on a success.

Week 1: Foundations
- Days 1 to 2: Indoors only. Practice the 'let's go' cue and reward him for standing next to you on a loose leash. Three or four sessions of five minutes each.
- Days 3 to 4: Harness and leash on, practicing in a hallway or another quiet space. Walk a few steps, stop if the leash goes tight, continue when it's slack. Reward often, roughly every few steps.
- Days 5 to 7: Quiet side streets. Ten-minute walks, two or three times a day. Use the stop-when-tight rule every single time. Add one or two 'go sniff' breaks per walk.

Week 2: More distance and distractions
- Days 8 to 9: Same quiet streets, but space out rewards to every ten or fifteen steps of loose leash. Walks can stretch to fifteen minutes if he's doing well.
- Days 10 to 11: Try a slightly busier route. Use higher value treats. Practice the step-aside-and-sit routine whenever something passes.
- Days 12 to 13: Try a short section of Cherry Creek at a quiet time. Keep it to five or ten minutes, then head back to an easier stretch.
- Day 14: Review. Pick whichever setting went best and do a relaxed, sniff-heavy walk as a reward for both of you.

Daily habits throughout:
- Every walk starts with a calm moment at the door. If he's bouncing, wait until he settles before you open it.
- Keep a consistent side. Pick left or right and always reward him on that side, at your leg.
- Don't worry about the destination. Early on you may only cover a block in ten minutes, and that's still progress.

If a day goes badly, just repeat the previous step for a day or two. Progress is rarely a straight line.
How will I know if it's working, or if I need to change something?

A few signs it's working:
- He checks in with you more, glancing back or slowing down when the leash gets close to tight.
- The leash spends more time in a loose J shape than pulled straight.
- You're stopping less often per block.
- He settles faster after distractions.

A simple way to track it: on one walk a day, count how many times you had to stop for pulling during the first five minutes. Jot the number down. Over a week or two it should trend down, even if some days are worse than others.

Signs you should adjust something:
1. You stop constantly and get almost nowhere. The setting is probably too hard. Go back to a quieter route for a few days.
2. He ignores treats outside. Either the treats aren't valuable enough there, or he's too excited. Upgrade the treat, or let him burn off some energy with play before the walk.
3. He pulls harder right after you start walking again. You might be setting off as soon as the leash goes slack but before he's actually turned toward you. Wait for a clear step back or a look.
4. Progress stalls after improving. That's usually a sign to raise the difficulty more slowly, or to practice in a wider variety of places.
5. He seems stressed: tail tucked, lip licking, yawning, refusing food. Make walks shorter and calmer for a while.

If things plateau for a few weeks, a session or two with a positive-reinforcement trainer can help a lot. They can watch your timing, which is hard to judge on your own.
This is really helpful, thanks.
Glad it helps. Consistency matters more than perfection, so even short, imperfect sessions add up. Good luck, and enjoy the walks with Biscuit.
My birthday's March 14 and I want to host dinner for eight people. Ideas? No satay though, I'm allergic to peanuts.

Happy early birthday! For eight people, a build-your-own taco night is easy and peanut-free: slow-cooked chicken tinga, black beans, rice, pickled onions, two salsas and warm tortillas. Or a pasta night: a big baked ziti, a green salad and garlic bread. Either way, check labels on sauces and desserts, since peanuts hide in some moles, granolas and baked goods. Want a shopping list?
Tacos! Yes please, a shopping list.

Here you go:
- 3 lb chicken thighs, 1 can chipotles in adobo, 2 onions, 1 head garlic
- 2 cans black beans, 2 cups rice
- 2 red onions and 6 limes for pickling
- Tomatillos and jalapeños for salsa verde; tomatoes for salsa roja
- 30 corn tortillas, cotija, cilantro, 4 avocados
- Dessert: churros or a tres leches cake (check the label)
How far ahead can I make the chicken tinga?

Tinga is a great make-ahead dish. It actually tastes better after a day in the fridge, because the chipotle and tomato flavors have time to settle in.

Timing options:
- Up to 2 days ahead: Cook it fully, cool it and refrigerate it covered. This is the sweet spot.
- Up to 3 months ahead: It freezes well. Freeze it in flat zip-top bags so it thaws faster, and thaw overnight in the fridge.
- Same day: Possible, but you'll be juggling it alongside everything else.

How to make it ahead:
1. Simmer the chicken thighs in salted water with a quartered onion and a couple of garlic cloves for about 25 minutes, until cooked through. Save the broth.
2. Shred the chicken with two forks.
3. Blend tomatoes (or a can of fire-roasted tomatoes), 2 to 3 chipotles plus a spoonful of the adobo, garlic, a pinch of oregano and a cup of the broth.
4. Saute a thinly sliced onion in oil until soft, pour in the sauce, simmer 10 minutes, then stir in the chicken and cook 5 more minutes.
5. Cool it quickly. Spread it in a shallow container rather than leaving it in the pot, and refrigerate within two hours.

Reheating on the day:
- Stovetop over medium-low with a splash of broth, stirring now and then, about 15 minutes.
- Or in a covered dish in a 325°F oven for 25 to 30 minutes.
- Taste after reheating. It often needs a little more salt and a squeeze of lime to wake it up.

Keep the extra broth in the fridge too. It's handy for loosening the tinga if it tightens up overnight. And with chipotles, start with fewer and add more after tasting, since the heat varies quite a bit between cans.
What's the best way to keep the tortillas warm for eight people?

With 30 corn tortillas, the goal is to heat them properly first, then hold them somewhere warm and a little steamy. Cold or dry corn tortillas crack, so both steps matter.

Heating:
- Best flavor: a dry skillet or griddle over medium-high, about 30 seconds per side, until they puff slightly and get a few toasted spots.
- Easier for a crowd: wrap stacks of 10 in damp paper towels, then in foil, and heat in a 300°F oven for 15 to 20 minutes.
- Microwave: stacks of 5 or 6 in a damp towel for 30 to 45 seconds. Fine in a pinch, but they get chewy as they cool.

Keeping them warm:
1. A tortilla warmer, cloth or insulated plastic, is cheap and works very well. It keeps a stack warm for 30 minutes or more.
2. No warmer? Wrap the stack in a clean kitchen towel and set it in a lidded pot or a small cooler. A cooler works surprisingly well as an insulated box.
3. Keep a second batch in the low oven in foil and swap stacks as people go through them, rather than putting all 30 out at once.

A few tips:
- With build-your-own tacos, people often eat three or four each, so 30 is about right for eight. A backup pack doesn't hurt.
- Double up tortillas for the tinga, since the sauce can soak through a single one.
- If you want a bit of theater, heat a stack on the griddle as guests arrive. The smell sets the mood.

If you'd like to offer a choice, a pack of small flour tortillas warmed the same way is a nice backup. Check the label, as you would for everything else.
Can you give me a timeline for the day of?

Here's a timeline that works backward from when guests arrive. Most of the work happens the day before, so the day itself stays calm.

The day before:
- Make the chicken tinga and refrigerate it.
- Make both salsas. They're better after the flavors meld overnight.
- Pickle the onions.
- Cook the beans if you're seasoning them from canned, then refrigerate.
- Set out serving bowls, spoons and platters, and label which dish goes where with sticky notes.

Morning of:
- Pick up anything fresh you still need: cilantro, avocados, limes.
- Chill drinks.
- Crumble the cotija and chop the cilantro, then store them covered in the fridge.

3 hours before guests arrive:
- Set the table or buffet area.
- Take dessert out of the fridge if it needs to come to room temperature.

90 minutes before:
- Start the rice. Once cooked, keep it covered off the heat; it holds for an hour.
- Tidy the kitchen and run the dishwasher so it's empty for later.

1 hour before:
- Start reheating the tinga on the stove or in the oven.
- Warm the beans on low.

30 minutes before:
- Wrap tortillas and put them in the oven to warm.
- Make the guacamole or slice the avocados, and squeeze lime over them so they don't brown.
- Put salsas, pickled onions, cotija and cilantro into serving bowls.

When guests arrive:
- Set out the toppings first, then bring out the hot dishes and tortillas once everyone is there.
- Keep the second batch of tortillas warming in the oven.

After dinner:
- Serve dessert and coffee.

The biggest thing is to keep the last hour light. If everything cold is done ahead, all you're doing is reheating and setting out bowls.
One guest is vegetarian. What can I add so they get a proper main and not just beans?

Good thinking. A few options that fit the taco spread and feel like a real main:

1. Mushroom tinga. Use the same chipotle tomato sauce, but with sliced mushrooms instead of chicken. Use vegetable broth instead of the chicken broth. It looks and tastes like it belongs with the rest, and meat eaters will probably try it too. Use about 1.5 lb of cremini or oyster mushrooms, seared in batches until browned before adding the sauce.

2. Roasted sweet potato and poblano. Cube two sweet potatoes, toss with oil, cumin, smoked paprika and salt, and roast at 425°F for about 25 minutes. Add strips of roasted poblano at the end. Great with the salsa verde.

3. Rajas con papas. Strips of roasted poblano with diced potatoes, onion and a splash of cream. Rich and comforting, and easy to keep warm in a covered pan.

Things to check so the rest of the table is vegetarian-friendly too:
- Rice: cook it in water or vegetable broth, not chicken broth.
- Beans: canned black beans are usually fine, but avoid refried beans made with lard.
- Serving spoons: give each dish its own spoon so the chicken doesn't end up in the vegetarian filling.
- Labels: small cards for each dish help everyone, and they're handy for flagging what's peanut-free too.

My pick would be the mushroom tinga. You're already making the sauce, so you can simply make a larger batch and split it into two pots before adding the chicken. It's the least extra work and it looks deliberate rather than like an afterthought.

Shopping list additions for the mushroom tinga:
- 1.5 lb mushrooms
- 1 extra onion
- 1 carton vegetable broth
- 1 extra can chipotles in adobo, if you want both pots equally smoky
Can I have the salsa verde recipe too?

Of course. This makes about 2 cups, which is plenty for eight.

Roasted salsa verde

Ingredients:
- 1 lb tomatillos, husked and rinsed
- 1 to 2 jalapenos (seed one for milder heat)
- 1/4 white onion, in a thick slice
- 2 garlic cloves, unpeeled
- 1/2 cup cilantro, loosely packed, stems included
- Juice of 1 lime
- 1 teaspoon salt, plus more to taste

Steps:
1. Heat your broiler with a rack about 4 inches from the top.
2. Put the tomatillos, jalapenos, onion and garlic on a foil-lined sheet pan.
3. Broil 5 to 7 minutes until blackened in spots, flip everything, and broil another 4 to 5 minutes. The tomatillos should be soft and slumped.
4. Let it cool for 10 minutes. Peel the garlic and pull the stems off the jalapenos.
5. Blend everything, including the juices from the pan, with the cilantro, lime juice and salt. Pulse rather than puree if you like it chunky.
6. Taste and adjust. More salt usually helps the most. If it's too sharp, a pinch of sugar rounds it out.

Notes:
- It thickens in the fridge as the pectin in the tomatillos sets. Stir in a spoonful of water before serving if needed.
- It keeps for about 5 days, so making it the day before is perfect.
- For a creamy version, blend in one avocado right before serving. Don't do this ahead or it'll brown.

For the salsa roja, you can use the same method with 5 or 6 Roma tomatoes, a jalapeno or a dried guajillo chile, onion and garlic. Having one green and one red gives the table nice contrast.
And the pickled onions?

These take about 10 minutes of work and are ready in an hour, though they're best after a night in the fridge.

Quick pickled red onions

Ingredients:
- 2 red onions, thinly sliced into rings or strips
- 3/4 cup apple cider vinegar or white vinegar
- 1/2 cup water
- 1 tablespoon sugar
- 1 1/2 teaspoons salt
- Optional: a few peppercorns, a bay leaf, a pinch of dried oregano, or a sliced jalapeno

Steps:
1. Pack the sliced onions into a clean jar or two.
2. Warm the vinegar, water, sugar and salt in a small pot just until the sugar and salt dissolve.
3. Pour the liquid over the onions, pressing them down so they're covered.
4. Let them sit at room temperature for 30 minutes to an hour, then refrigerate.

Lime version:
Since you're buying limes anyway, you can do the more traditional Yucatan-style version. Toss the onions with the juice of 5 or 6 limes, a teaspoon of salt and a pinch of oregano. Pour boiling water over the onions first, drain after 30 seconds, then add the lime juice. They turn bright pink within a few hours.

Tips:
- Slice the onions as thinly as you can. A mandoline helps, but a sharp knife is fine.
- They keep for about 2 weeks in the fridge.
- They're great on the mushroom tinga too, since the acidity cuts through the richness.

With the salsas and onions done the day before, your cold toppings are basically finished before the party even starts.
Amazing, thank you!
You're welcome! With the make-ahead plan, you'll get to actually enjoy your own birthday dinner instead of being stuck at the stove. Have a wonderful time.
I'm a barista at Lark Café and I got roped into making our shift schedule. Seven of us, open 6am to 6pm. Can you help me set up a spreadsheet?

Sure. Use a grid with days across the top and shifts down the side: Open 6–12, Mid 10–4, Close 12–6. Put names in the cells. Add a second tab that totals hours per person with COUNTIF, so nobody goes over. Color-code openers and closers so gaps jump out.
Can you put me on later shifts when possible? I bike in, it's about 10 minutes, and I'd rather not ride in the dark at 5:30.

Makes sense. I'll put you on mid and closing shifts first. Here's a starting week:
- Mon: Open Sam, Mid Nell, Close Jo
- Tue: Open Ana, Mid Lee, Close Nell
- Wed: Open Sam, Mid Nell, Close Raf
and so on. Want the hours tab formula too?
Yes please, the hours formula.

Here's a setup that works in both Google Sheets and Excel.

Schedule tab layout:
- A1 is blank. B1 through H1 are the days: Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun.
- A2 is Open (6-12), A3 is Mid (10-4), A4 is Close (12-6).
- B2:H4 hold the names.

Hours tab layout:
- Column A lists everyone: Sam, Jo, Ana, Lee, Raf, Nell, and your seventh teammate.
- Column B is shift count.
- Column C is total hours.

Formulas:
- In B2: =COUNTIF(Schedule!$B$2:$H$4, A2)
- In C2: =B2*6
- Fill both down for all seven rows.

Since every shift is exactly six hours, counting shifts and multiplying by six is all you need. If you ever add shifts of different lengths, switch to one COUNTIF per row type:
=COUNTIF(Schedule!$B$2:$H$2, A2)*6 + COUNTIF(Schedule!$B$3:$H$3, A2)*6 + COUNTIF(Schedule!$B$4:$H$4, A2)*6
Then change each 6 to that shift's length.

Adding a limit check:
1. Put the maximum weekly hours in a cell, say E1, and label it in D1 as Max hours.
2. Select C2:C8 and add conditional formatting with a custom formula: =C2>$E$1
3. Set it to fill red. Anyone over the limit lights up immediately.

A coverage check is worth adding too:
- In the Hours tab, put =COUNTA(Schedule!B2:H4) somewhere and label it Shifts filled. With three shifts a day for seven days, a complete week shows 21.
- If it's lower, there's a gap somewhere.

One gotcha: COUNTIF is exact-match but not case-sensitive, and it does care about extra spaces. If someone types 'Sam ' with a trailing space, it won't count. Data validation fixes this; I can walk you through it if you'd like.
Can you fill out the rest of the week? Everyone should get about the same number of shifts.

Sure. With 21 shifts and seven people, that works out to exactly three shifts each. I kept the first three days as we had them, kept you on mid and close shifts, and avoided anyone closing one night and opening the next morning.

- Mon: Open Sam, Mid Nell, Close Jo
- Tue: Open Ana, Mid Lee, Close Nell
- Wed: Open Sam, Mid Nell, Close Raf
- Thu: Open Ana, Mid [Staff 7], Close Jo
- Fri: Open Lee, Mid Raf, Close [Staff 7]
- Sat: Open Jo, Mid [Staff 7], Close Ana
- Sun: Open Raf, Mid Sam, Close Lee

Shift counts:
- Sam: 3 (Open, Open, Mid)
- Jo: 3 (Close, Close, Open)
- Ana: 3 (Open, Open, Close)
- Lee: 3 (Mid, Open, Close)
- Raf: 3 (Close, Mid, Open)
- Nell: 3 (Mid, Close, Mid)
- [Staff 7]: 3 (Mid, Close, Mid)

I used [Staff 7] as a placeholder for the seventh person; just swap in their name and the Hours tab will update on its own.

A few things I checked:
- Every day has all three shifts covered.
- No one works two shifts on the same day.
- No close-then-open pairs. Jo closes Thursday and opens Saturday, with Friday off between.
- Most people get a mix of shift types, so no one is stuck opening every time.

Things you might want to tweak:
- Weekends are often busier. If that's true for you, you could add a second Mid on Saturday and Sunday, which would bump a couple of people to four shifts.
- If anyone prefers consistency, like always opening, it's easy to rearrange as long as the counts stay balanced.

Want me to lay it out as rows and columns you can paste straight into the sheet?
Can the sheet flag it automatically if someone closes and then opens the next morning?

Yes, with conditional formatting. The idea is to compare each Open cell with the Close cell from the day before.

Using the layout above (days in B1:H1, Open in row 2, Close in row 4):

1. Select C2:H2, which is the Open row from Tuesday through Sunday.
2. Go to Format, then Conditional formatting.
3. Choose Custom formula and enter:
=AND(C2<>"", C2=B4)
4. Pick a bright fill, like orange.

Because the references are relative, the rule for Tuesday's Open (C2) checks Monday's Close (B4), Wednesday's Open (D2) checks Tuesday's Close (C4), and so on.

It's also nice to highlight the matching Close cell so both ends of the problem stand out:
1. Select B4:G4, the Close row from Monday through Saturday.
2. Custom formula: =AND(B4<>"", B4=C2)
3. Same color.

The Sunday-to-Monday gap:
That one crosses weeks, so it depends on how you store them. If each week is its own tab, add a cell on the new week's tab that pulls last Sunday's closer, for example in J4:
='Last week'!H4
Then add a rule on B2: =AND(B2<>"", B2=$J$4)

If you keep weeks stacked on one tab, one under the other, you can point the Monday rule at the Sunday Close cell in the block above instead.

A simpler fallback is a check cell that counts problems. In any empty cell:
=SUMPRODUCT((C2:H2<>"")*(C2:H2=B4:G4))
If it shows anything above zero, there's a close-then-open somewhere. Label it 'Clopens' and you can glance at it before sending the schedule out.
Some people can't work certain days. What's a good way to track that in the sheet?

Add an Availability tab and have the Schedule tab check against it.

Availability tab layout:
- A1 is blank. B1 through H1 are Mon through Sun, matching the Schedule tab exactly.
- A2 through A8 list everyone's names, spelled exactly as they appear on the schedule.
- In each cell, put X if that person can't work that day. Leave it blank if they can.

If people have shift-level limits, like 'no opens on Monday', you can use letters instead of X: O for can't open, C for can't close, X for can't work at all.

Flagging conflicts on the Schedule tab:
1. Select B2:H4 on the Schedule tab.
2. Add conditional formatting with a custom formula:
=IFERROR(INDEX(Availability!$B$2:$H$8, MATCH(B2, Availability!$A$2:$A$8, 0), COLUMN(B2)-1)="X", FALSE)
3. Choose a red fill.

What that does: MATCH finds the person's row on the Availability tab, COLUMN(B2)-1 picks the matching day, and INDEX checks whether that cell is X. IFERROR keeps empty cells or typos from causing errors.

Note: in Google Sheets, conditional formatting can't always reference other tabs directly. If the rule doesn't work, wrap the range in INDIRECT:
INDIRECT("Availability!B2:H8") and INDIRECT("Availability!A2:A8")

Making data entry easier:
- On the Schedule tab, add data validation to B2:H4 with 'list from a range' pointing at Availability!A2:A8. Now every cell is a dropdown of names, which also solves the trailing-space problem from before.
- Add a Notes column on the Availability tab for things that don't fit the grid, like 'prefers mornings' or 'max three shifts'.

Ask everyone to update their own row by a set day each week. That way you're not chasing people by text, and the red cells tell you right away if a draft won't work.
Could you write a short message I can send the team with the schedule?

Here's a friendly, clear version:

'Hi all! Here's the schedule for next week at Lark Café. Link: [sheet link]

A few quick notes:
- Please double-check your shifts and let me know by [day] if something doesn't work.
- If you need to swap, trade with someone directly, then add it to the Swaps tab so the schedule stays accurate.
- There's now an Availability tab. Please mark any days you can't work for the following week by [day], so I can plan around them.

Thanks, everyone!
Nell'

If you'd like something shorter for a group chat:

'Next week's schedule is up: [sheet link]. Check your shifts, mark any days you can't work on the Availability tab by [day], and log any swaps on the Swaps tab. Thanks!'

A few tips for sending it:
- Share the sheet as view-only for the Schedule tab and editable for Availability and Swaps. In Google Sheets you can protect individual tabs under Data, then Protect sheets and ranges.
- Pin the message, or post it at the same time each week, so people know when to look.
- Keep the deadline for availability a few days before you build the next schedule, which gives you time to sort out conflicts.

I mentioned a Swaps tab in the message. Want me to set that up too?
Yes, how should the swaps tab work?

Keep it simple, so people actually use it.

Swaps tab columns:
- A: Day (dropdown: Mon through Sun)
- B: Shift (dropdown: Open, Mid, Close)
- C: Original person (dropdown of names)
- D: Covering person (dropdown of names)
- E: Approved (checkbox)
- F: Notes

Set the dropdowns with data validation, using the same name list from the Availability tab, so spelling stays consistent.

How it flows:
1. The two people agree on a swap between themselves.
2. One of them adds a row to the Swaps tab.
3. You check it for problems, such as overtime or a close-then-open, and tick Approved.
4. You update the Schedule tab.

Optional: make the Schedule update itself.
If you'd rather not edit the schedule by hand, keep a 'Base' tab with the original plan and make the visible Schedule tab show the swapped name when there's an approved swap. In Schedule!B2 you'd use something like:
=IFERROR(INDEX(FILTER(Swaps!$D:$D, Swaps!$A:$A=B$1, Swaps!$B:$B=$A2, Swaps!$E:$E=TRUE), 1), Base!B2)
That looks for an approved swap matching the day and shift, and falls back to the original name if there isn't one. Fill it across B2:H4.

This is a nice touch, but it adds complexity. For seven people, editing by hand is honestly fine.

Ground rules worth writing at the top of the tab:
- Swaps need to be logged before the shift, not after.
- The covering person must check the Availability tab first.
- Once a swap is approved, the covering person is responsible for the shift.

With Schedule, Hours, Availability and Swaps, you have a complete little system. The hours and close-then-open checks will catch most mistakes before anyone notices.
Perfect. Thanks so much.
You're welcome! Once it's set up, each new week should mostly be a matter of duplicating the tab and swapping a few names. Good luck with the first one.
I'm trying to switch into UX design. Where should I start with Figma?

Good plan. Start with frames, auto layout and components: those three cover most real work. For a first project, redesign a screen you use every day. Then write a short case study: the problem, sketches, a wireframe, a clickable prototype, and what you'd test. Figma's own tutorials and the community files are free and good.
Ha, I could redesign the ordering tablet at work. Everyone hates it.
That's a great case study: you have real users and real pain points. Interview two or three coworkers, write down their top complaints, then design a fix and test it with them.
How should I run the interviews with coworkers? What should I ask?

Keep them short and casual: 15 to 20 minutes each, one person at a time. The goal is to hear about real moments with the tablet, not opinions about what it should look like.

Before you start:
- Tell them it's for a learning project, there are no wrong answers, and you're not testing them.
- Ask if you can take notes. Write down their exact words where you can; quotes are gold for a case study later.

Questions to ask:
1. Walk me through the last time you used the tablet to take an order. What happened?
2. What's the most annoying part of using it?
3. Can you remember a time it slowed you down or caused a mistake? What happened next?
4. Are there workarounds you use, like shortcuts, notes or doing something outside the tablet?
5. What do new people struggle with most when they learn it?
6. If you could change one thing about it, what would it be?
7. Is there anything it does well that you'd want to keep?

Follow-up prompts to dig deeper:
- 'Can you show me?' If possible, have them demonstrate on the tablet. Watching beats listening.
- 'Why do you think that happens?'
- 'How often does that come up?'
- 'What did you do then?'

Things to avoid:
- Leading questions like 'Wouldn't it be better if the buttons were bigger?' Ask 'What do you think of the buttons?' instead, or better, don't ask about buttons at all and see if they bring it up.
- Pitching your own ideas mid-interview. Save them for later.
- Asking people to predict what they'd use. People are better at describing past behavior than future behavior.

Right after each interview, spend five minutes writing up the top three things you heard while it's fresh. Those quick summaries make the next step much easier.
Once I have their complaints, how do I turn that into a design?

This is where a lot of first projects skip a step, so it's worth doing deliberately. The path is roughly: notes, themes, problems, ideas, design.

1. Affinity mapping
Write each observation or quote on its own sticky note, physical or in FigJam. One idea per note. Then group them by similarity without deciding the groups ahead of time. You'll end up with clusters like 'finding items', 'editing an order', 'payment confusion'. Name each cluster.

2. Pick the biggest problems
For each cluster, ask: how often does it happen, and how bad is it when it does? Something that happens on every order and adds a few seconds can matter more than a rare crash. Choose two or three to focus on. A tight scope makes a better case study than trying to fix everything.

3. Write problem statements
For each one, write a single sentence: '[Who] needs a way to [do something] because [reason].' For example: 'Staff need a way to change an item in an order without starting over, because rebuilding the order during a rush causes mistakes.'

4. Sketch lots of options
On paper, fast and ugly. Aim for several different approaches per problem, not variations of one. Crazy Eights is a good exercise: fold a sheet into eight panels and sketch eight ideas in eight minutes.

5. Pick and refine
Choose the most promising idea for each problem and turn it into a rough wireframe in Figma. Grayscale, simple boxes, real labels. Don't worry about colors or fonts yet.

6. Map the flow
Before polishing screens, lay out the steps of a full order from start to finish. This shows where your fixes fit and whether you've introduced new problems.

Keep photos of the sticky notes and sketches. Messy process artifacts are exactly what hiring managers like to see in a case study, because they show how you think.
Can you explain auto layout more simply? I keep getting confused by it.

Sure. Think of auto layout as a box that arranges its contents for you, like a stack.

The core idea:
Without auto layout, every element sits at a fixed position. If you change a button label from 'Add' to 'Add to order', the text overflows and you have to resize the button by hand. With auto layout, the button grows to fit the text on its own.

The four settings that matter:
1. Direction: stack items vertically (one above the other) or horizontally (side by side).
2. Gap: the space between each item.
3. Padding: the space between the edge of the box and the items inside.
4. Alignment: where items sit inside the box, like top left or centered.

Resizing, which is where most confusion comes from:
Each element inside an auto layout frame has a width and height setting:
- Hug contents: shrink to fit whatever is inside. Good for buttons and tags.
- Fill container: stretch to take up the available space. Good for a text field or a card in a list.
- Fixed: stay at an exact size, no matter what.

A practice exercise:
1. Make a text layer that says 'Add to order'.
2. Select it and press Shift + A. Figma wraps it in an auto layout frame.
3. Set padding to 12 on top and bottom, 20 on the sides. Give the frame a fill color and corner radius. You now have a button.
4. Edit the text. Watch the button resize itself.
5. Duplicate the button twice, select all three, and press Shift + A again. Now you have a horizontal row of buttons with even spacing.
6. Change the direction to vertical and see what happens.

The mental model that helps most: frames inside frames. A screen is a vertical stack. Inside it, a header is a horizontal stack. Inside that, a button is a tiny stack with one text layer. Once you see layouts that way, auto layout starts to feel natural.
Okay, that helps. What about components and variants?

Components are reusable pieces. Variants are different versions of the same component.

Components
When you make something into a component (select it and press Ctrl + Alt + K on Windows, or Cmd + Option + K on a Mac), it becomes the main component. Every copy you place is an instance. If you change the main component, every instance updates.

Why it matters: if your order screen has 20 item buttons and you decide they need bigger text, you change one thing instead of 20.

You can still customize instances. Change the label text, swap an icon, or hide a layer, and those overrides stay put even when the main component updates.

Variants
Variants group related versions of a component into one set, with properties you can switch between. For example, a button might have:
- State: Default, Pressed, Disabled
- Style: Primary, Secondary

Instead of six separate components, you have one button with two dropdowns in the right panel.

How to make them:
1. Build your default button with auto layout.
2. Make it a component.
3. In the right panel, click the button to add a variant. Figma duplicates it inside a dashed purple box.
4. Change the duplicate's look, for example darker for Pressed.
5. Rename the property and values in the right panel so they make sense.

Components worth building for the ordering tablet project:
- Menu item button: with states for default, selected and unavailable.
- Order line: item name, modifiers, price, and an edit or delete action.
- Category tab: default and active.
- Primary and secondary buttons.
- A modal or bottom sheet for editing an item.

A tip: keep your components on their own page in the file, called something like 'Components'. It keeps your screens tidy, and it looks organized if you share the file with anyone reviewing your work.
How do I make a clickable prototype so I can test it with coworkers?

Figma's Prototype tab makes this pretty approachable.

Setting it up:
1. Make a frame for each screen in the flow you want to test, for example: home, item selected, editing an item, order review, order sent.
2. Size the frames to match the tablet. If you're not sure of the exact size, pick a close tablet preset from the Frame tool.
3. Switch to the Prototype tab in the right panel.
4. Select a button, then drag the little circle that appears onto the screen it should lead to. That creates a connection.
5. Set the trigger (usually On tap) and the animation. Instant or Dissolve is fine for testing; fancy transitions just distract.
6. Set a starting frame by selecting the first screen and adding a flow starting point.

Useful extras:
- Overlays: for pop-ups like an edit dialog, set the connection to Open overlay instead of Navigate to.
- Back actions: connect close buttons to Back so you don't need to wire every path.
- Interactive components: if your buttons have Pressed variants, you can make them change state on tap inside the component, and every instance inherits it.

Running the test:
- Open the prototype on an actual tablet if you can, using the Figma mobile app or a browser link. It feels much closer to the real thing than a laptop.
- Give each person a realistic task, like 'Take an order for two items, then change one of them.' Don't explain how.
- Ask them to think out loud.
- Stay quiet and watch where they hesitate. Resist helping unless they're completely stuck.
- Afterward ask: 'What was easy? What was confusing? How does this compare to the current tablet?'

If you can, time the same task on the old tablet and on your prototype. Even rough numbers make a case study much stronger. Note them down along with any quotes.
And what should the case study write-up look like? Can you give me an outline?

Here's an outline that works well for a first case study. Aim for something people can skim in five minutes, heavy on visuals and light on paragraphs.

1. Title and summary
A one-line title, like 'Redesigning an ordering tablet staff actually like', followed by a short summary: the problem, your role, the timeframe, and the outcome.

2. The problem
What was wrong with the current tablet and why it mattered. Include a screenshot or photo of the original and one or two strong quotes from interviews.

3. Research
Who you talked to and how. Show your affinity map and the main themes you found. Keep the method brief; the insights are what matter.

4. Problem statements
The two or three problems you chose to focus on, and why those and not others.

5. Ideas and sketches
Photos of your sketches, including ideas you rejected and why. This shows judgment.

6. Wireframes and iteration
Low-fidelity screens, then what changed as you refined them. Before and after comparisons work great here.

7. Final design
Your polished screens with short annotations explaining key decisions. A short screen recording or GIF of the prototype is a nice touch.

8. Testing and results
What happened when people used it. Task times, quotes, what worked, what didn't, and what you changed afterward.

9. What I'd do next
Things you'd test or build with more time. This shows you understand design is ongoing.

10. Reflection
A few sentences on what you learned about the process.

Formatting tips:
- Lead every section with a short heading and one sentence that says the takeaway.
- Use real screenshots instead of describing things.
- Keep it honest. A small project explained clearly beats an inflated one.

You can publish it on a simple portfolio site or even as a well-formatted PDF to start. The content matters far more than the platform.
This is great, thanks!
You're welcome! Feel free to come back when you have sketches or a first prototype and want feedback.
Can you help with a cover letter for a junior UX designer job at Fernhill Studio? I still work at Lark Café, and I want to say what it taught me about people.

Here's an opening: "For three years I've watched people make decisions at a café counter: in a hurry, distracted, sometimes confused by a menu. At Lark Café I learned to notice where people hesitate, and to fix it." Then a paragraph on your ordering-tablet redesign: who you interviewed, what you changed, and what happened. Close with why Fernhill in particular.
Love it. Can you make the ending less formal?
"I'd love to bring the same habit of watching, listening and fixing to Fernhill. Thanks for reading. I hope we get to talk."
Can you put the whole letter together as one full draft?

Here's a full draft. I've used brackets where you'll want to fill in specifics, since the details of your project should come from you.

Dear Fernhill Studio team,

For three years I've watched people make decisions at a café counter: in a hurry, distracted, sometimes confused by a menu. At Lark Café I learned to notice where people hesitate, and to fix it. I'm applying for the junior UX designer role because I want to do that work on purpose, every day.

The clearest example is the ordering tablet we use behind the counter. Almost everyone on staff found it frustrating, so I made it a project. I interviewed [number] coworkers about how they actually used it and watched them take real orders. The same problems came up again and again: [problem one] and [problem two]. [Describe the result, for example how much faster a task became or what testers said.] The biggest lesson was that the people using a tool every day already know what's wrong with it; my job is to listen closely and turn that into something clear.

Working a busy counter has also taught me things that don't show up in a portfolio. I'm used to explaining things simply to people who are short on time, staying calm when something breaks in the middle of a rush, and getting honest feedback, fast.

I'm drawn to Fernhill because [something specific about the studio's work, values or clients]. [One sentence on how that connects to what you care about.]

I'd love to bring the same habit of watching, listening and fixing to Fernhill. Thanks for reading. I hope we get to talk.

Best,
Nell [Last name]
[Portfolio link]

A couple of notes:
- If the posting names a hiring manager, use their name instead of 'Fernhill Studio team'.
- The project paragraph is the heart of the letter. Concrete details, like what you changed and one real quote from a tester, will do more than any adjective.
Is it too long? How long should a cover letter be?

It's in a good range, but there's room to tighten. The usual guidance:

- Length: 250 to 400 words, comfortably under one page.
- Paragraphs: three to five, each with one clear job.
- Reading time: under a minute. Many people skim the first and last paragraphs first, so those need to land on their own.

The draft above is around 300 words before you fill in the brackets, so once you add details it could creep toward the upper end. The easiest place to trim is the third paragraph, since the project already shows most of those qualities.

Here's a tighter version, about 220 words plus your specifics:

Dear Fernhill Studio team,

For three years I've watched people make decisions at a café counter: in a hurry, distracted, sometimes confused by a menu. At Lark Café I learned to notice where people hesitate, and to fix it. I'm applying for the junior UX designer role because I want to do that work on purpose.

The ordering tablet behind our counter frustrated almost everyone on staff, so I made it a project. I interviewed [number] coworkers, watched them take real orders, and found two recurring problems: [problem one] and [problem two]. I sketched options, built a clickable prototype and tested it with the same people. [Result.] The lesson I keep coming back to: the people using a tool every day already know what's wrong with it. I'm drawn to Fernhill because [specific reason]. 

I'd love to bring the same habit of watching, listening and fixing to Fernhill. Thanks for reading. I hope we get to talk.

Best,
Nell [Last name]
[Portfolio link]

If you'd like to keep one line from the cut paragraph, the one about explaining things simply to people who are short on time is the strongest. It could go right after the result sentence.
How do I find something specific about Fernhill to mention? I don't want it to sound generic.

Good instinct. The 'why this company' line is where most cover letters go vague, and it's the easiest place to stand out.

Where to look:
1. Their portfolio or case studies. Pick one project and note something specific about how they approached it, not just that it looks nice.
2. Their blog, newsletter or talks. Studios often write about their process. A line about how they do research or work with clients is great material.
3. The job posting itself. Look for phrases about what they value, like 'close collaboration with clients' or 'research-led'. Echo one, in your own words, with an example.
4. Their social media. Recent launches or team posts can give you something current to mention.
5. Their 'About' page. Values or a mission statement can work, but only if you connect them to something real you've done.

How to write the line:
A good pattern is: what they did, plus why it resonates with you, plus a link to your experience.

Examples using placeholders:
- 'I was struck by your [project name] case study, especially how you [specific step]. That's the same approach I tried with the ordering tablet, and I'd love to learn to do it at a higher level.'
- 'Your post on [topic] put into words something I'd noticed behind the counter: [short idea]. That's why Fernhill is at the top of my list.'
- 'The posting mentions [phrase]. That's the part of design I enjoy most, and it's what I did when [brief example].'

Things to avoid:
- Compliments that could apply to any studio, like 'innovative', 'creative' or 'great culture'.
- Overclaiming. Saying you've followed them for years when you haven't is easy to see through.
- Listing several projects. One specific reference beats three vague ones.

Spend twenty or thirty minutes on their site and jot down two or three possibilities. Then pick the one you can connect most naturally to your own project.
Can you give me a subject line and a short email to send it with?

Sure. Check the posting first in case they ask for a specific subject format or reference number. If not, these work well:

Subject line options:
- Junior UX Designer application: Nell [Last name]
- Application for Junior UX Designer, Nell [Last name]
- Junior UX Designer role, portfolio and cover letter attached

The first is the clearest and easiest to search for later.

Email body:

Hi [name or Fernhill Studio team],

I'm applying for the Junior UX Designer role at Fernhill Studio. My cover letter and résumé are attached, and you can see my work here: [portfolio link].

My main case study is a redesign of the ordering tablet at Lark Café, based on interviews and testing with the staff who use it every day.

Thanks for your time. I'd be glad to talk more.

Best,
Nell [Last name]
[Portfolio link]

A few practical tips:
- Attach the cover letter and résumé as PDFs, not Word files, so the formatting stays put.
- Name the files clearly, like 'Nell-Lastname-Cover-Letter.pdf' and 'Nell-Lastname-Resume.pdf'.
- Some people paste the cover letter into the email body instead of attaching it. Either is fine, but don't do both. If the posting doesn't say, attaching is cleaner.
- Send it to yourself first to check that the links work and the attachments open.

If they use an application form instead of email, the same email text works well in any 'additional information' box.
What should I double-check before I send it?

Here's a final checklist.

Content:
- Every bracket is filled in. Search the document for '[' to be sure.
- The company name is spelled correctly everywhere, including in the file names.
- The role title matches the posting exactly.
- The project paragraph includes at least one concrete detail: a number, a quote, or a specific change.
- The 'why Fernhill' line is specific to them and couldn't be pasted into another letter.

Tone and length:
- Read it out loud. Anything that sounds stiff or that you'd never say probably needs rewording.
- It fits on one page with comfortable margins.
- The first sentence and last paragraph make sense on their own, for skimmers.

Links and files:
- The portfolio link works in a private browser window, not only when you're logged in.
- The case study it leads to is finished and easy to find.
- Attachments are PDFs, open correctly, and have clear file names.

Details people miss:
- Consistent formatting: one font, one size, no stray bold.
- Consistent spelling of words that have variants.
- Typos in names, especially the hiring manager's, if you used one.
- The date or reference number, if the posting asked for one.

Last steps:
- Have someone else read it if you can. Fresh eyes catch things yours won't.
- Send it to yourself one more time and look at it on your phone.
- Keep a copy of the letter and the posting together, so you can review both before an interview.

Once all of that checks out, send it. Don't hold it back trying to make it perfect; a clear, honest letter with a solid project is already better than most.

Correction from before: it's tree nuts I'm allergic to, not peanuts. Peanuts are fine. Can you suggest swaps for a pesto recipe?

Thanks for correcting that. Classic pesto uses pine nuts, which many people with tree-nut allergies tolerate but some don't, so check with your doctor. Safe swaps: toasted sunflower or pumpkin seeds, or leave the nuts out and add more parmesan. Watch out for store-bought walnut or cashew pestos.
Sunflower seeds it is.
Good choice. Toast them for two minutes in a dry pan first; they get a nutty flavor without the nuts.
Can you give me the full pesto recipe with the sunflower seeds worked in?

Here's a straightforward version that makes about one cup, enough for a pound of pasta.

Ingredients:
- 2 packed cups fresh basil leaves, stems pulled off
- 1/3 cup raw sunflower seeds, toasted
- 1 to 2 garlic cloves, depending on how strong you like it
- 1/2 cup finely grated parmesan
- 1/2 cup good olive oil, plus a little extra
- 1 to 2 teaspoons lemon juice
- Salt to taste

Steps:
1. Toast the seeds. Put them in a dry skillet over medium heat and stir often for two to three minutes, until they smell toasty and a few turn light golden. Tip them onto a plate right away so they don't keep cooking in the hot pan.
2. Blend the base. Add the cooled seeds and garlic to a food processor and pulse until they look like coarse sand.
3. Add the basil. Pack it in and pulse in short bursts, scraping down the sides, until it's finely chopped.
4. Stream in the oil. With the machine running, pour the oil in slowly until the pesto is loose and glossy.
5. Finish by hand. Transfer to a bowl and stir in the parmesan and lemon juice. Taste and add salt a pinch at a time; parmesan is salty, so you may need less than you think.

To serve with pasta, save a mug of the cooking water before draining. Toss the pasta with the pesto off the heat and add splashes of pasta water until it coats every strand. Heat dulls basil fast, so never cook the pesto in the pan.
Why does pesto always turn dark after a day?

That's oxidation. Cut basil leaves release enzymes that react with air and turn the green to a muddy olive color. It's harmless, but there are a few ways to slow it down:

1. Blanch the basil. Drop the leaves into boiling water for about ten seconds, then straight into ice water. Squeeze them dry in a towel before blending. This deactivates the browning enzymes and keeps the color bright for days. The flavor is a touch milder, but most people can't tell.
2. Add acid. The lemon juice in the recipe helps a little. Don't overdo it or it will taste sour.
3. Cover the surface. Pack the pesto into a jar, smooth the top, and pour a thin layer of olive oil over it so no air touches the sauce. Press plastic wrap directly onto the surface if you don't want the extra oil.
4. Keep it cold. Refrigerate it as soon as it's made, and use it within about five days.
5. Add parmesan later. If you're making pesto to store, leave the cheese out and stir it in just before serving. Cheese-free pesto keeps and freezes better.

If you only do one thing, do the blanching. It makes the biggest difference.
Can I freeze it?

Yes, pesto freezes very well. Here's the method that works best:

1. Make it without the cheese. Parmesan can turn a bit grainy in the freezer, and it's easy to stir in fresh later.
2. Use an ice cube tray. Spoon the pesto into the cubes, smooth the tops, and drizzle a little oil over each one to stop browning.
3. Freeze until solid, usually four to six hours, then pop the cubes out and store them in a labeled freezer bag with as much air pressed out as possible.
4. Portioning: one standard cube is about two tablespoons, which is a good amount for a single serving of pasta. Three or four cubes will dress a pound.
5. Storage time: the flavor stays good for about three months. It's still safe after that, but the basil gets duller.
6. Thawing: drop frozen cubes straight into a bowl with hot drained pasta and a splash of pasta water and stir; they melt in under a minute. For sandwiches or dips, thaw cubes in the fridge overnight.

Once thawed, stir in the parmesan and taste for salt and lemon before serving.
What else can the sunflower seeds go in? Recipes that usually call for nuts.

Toasted sunflower seeds and pumpkin seeds are two of the most flexible swaps in the kitchen. Here are places they work well:

1. Granola. Swap the nuts one for one with a mix of sunflower and pumpkin seeds. Add them in the last ten minutes of baking so they don't scorch.
2. Salad toppings. Toss toasted seeds with a pinch of salt and smoked paprika for a crunchy topping on green salads, grain bowls, or roasted vegetables.
3. Crumb crusts. For a fish or chicken crust that would normally use chopped nuts, pulse sunflower seeds with breadcrumbs, parmesan, and herbs.
4. Seed butter. Sunflower seed butter works in place of other nut butters in sauces, smoothies, and baking. Blend toasted seeds in a food processor for eight to ten minutes, scraping often, until creamy, then add salt and a little oil if it's stiff.
5. Baked goods. In muffins, banana bread, and cookies, use toasted seeds in the same amount as chopped nuts. One quirk: sunflower seeds can turn green inside baked goods when they react with baking soda. It's harmless chlorophyll chemistry. Reducing the baking soda slightly or adding a little lemon juice helps.
6. Dukkah. This Egyptian spice-and-crunch mix is traditionally made with hazelnuts, but toasted seeds make a great version. Sprinkle it on eggs, avocado toast, roasted carrots, or bread dipped in olive oil.
7. Trail mix. Combine seeds with dried fruit, toasted coconut flakes, and chocolate chips.

Always check the packaging on seeds you buy, since some are processed in facilities that also handle nuts.
The dukkah sounds good. Can you write that one out properly?

Sure. This makes about one cup.

Ingredients:
- 1/2 cup raw sunflower seeds
- 1/4 cup raw pumpkin seeds
- 3 tablespoons sesame seeds
- 2 tablespoons coriander seeds
- 1 tablespoon cumin seeds
- 1 teaspoon fennel seeds (optional)
- 1 teaspoon flaky salt, or 3/4 teaspoon fine salt
- 1/2 teaspoon chili flakes or sweet paprika

Steps:
1. Toast the big seeds. In a dry skillet over medium heat, toast the sunflower and pumpkin seeds for three to four minutes, stirring, until the pumpkin seeds start to puff and pop. Tip them onto a plate.
2. Toast the sesame. Toast the sesame seeds in the same pan for about a minute, until golden. They burn quickly, so watch them. Add them to the plate.
3. Toast the spices. Toast the coriander, cumin, and fennel for about a minute, just until fragrant.
4. Cool everything. Let it all cool completely, or the mix will turn pasty when you grind it.
5. Grind. Pulse the spices in a spice grinder or crush them in a mortar until coarse. Then add the sunflower and pumpkin seeds and pulse just a few times. You want a crumbly, sandy mix with some texture, not a powder.
6. Season. Stir in the sesame, salt, and chili flakes. Taste and adjust.

Ways to use it: the classic is bread dipped first in olive oil, then in dukkah. It's also great on fried or soft-boiled eggs, avocado toast, roasted vegetables, yogurt dips, and as a crust on fish. Store it in an airtight jar at room temperature for about two weeks, or in the fridge for a month.
Can pesto be made without a food processor?

Yes, and some people think it's even better. There are three good options:

1. Mortar and pestle (the traditional way). Pound the garlic with a pinch of coarse salt into a paste first. Add the toasted seeds and pound until finely crushed. Add the basil a handful at a time, grinding in a circular motion rather than smashing straight down; the salt helps break the leaves. Stir in the cheese, then the oil a little at a time. It takes about ten minutes, and the texture is creamier and less watery than machine-made pesto because the leaves are crushed rather than sliced.

2. Blender. A blender works but needs more liquid to keep things turning over. Put the oil in first, then the garlic and seeds, then the basil. Pulse rather than running it continuously, and stop to push things down with a spatula. Don't let it run long, or the friction heats the basil and dulls the color.

3. Knife and board. Chop the garlic finely, then add the seeds and chop until they're like coarse crumbs. Pile the basil on top and keep rocking the knife through everything until it's very fine. Scrape it into a bowl and stir in the cheese and oil. You'll end up with a chunkier, rustic pesto that's great on bread or stirred into soup.

Whichever you pick, toasting the seeds first matters more than the tool. It's where most of the flavor comes from.
Last question: what if I run out of basil?

Pesto is really a method, not a single recipe, so lots of greens work. Keep the rest of the formula the same (seeds, garlic, cheese, oil, lemon, salt) and swap the leaves:

1. Spinach. Mild and cheap. Use it alone, or mix it in roughly equal parts with whatever basil you have to stretch it.
2. Arugula. Sharp and bold. Great with pasta or as a sandwich spread. Add a little extra lemon to balance the bite.
3. Kale. Strip the stems and blanch the leaves for a minute first so they soften. It makes a hearty, dark green pesto that holds up well in the fridge.
4. Parsley and cilantro. Both make bright, herby sauces. Cilantro with pumpkin seeds, lime instead of lemon, and a little jalapeño is excellent on tacos or grilled vegetables.
5. Carrot tops. Don't throw them out. They're slightly earthy and taste good mixed with parsley.
6. Mint. Too strong alone, but a small handful with parsley makes a pesto that goes well with lamb, peas, or roasted carrots.

General tips:
- Tougher greens need a quick blanch; tender herbs don't.
- Bitter greens like arugula and kale benefit from extra cheese or a teaspoon of honey.
- Taste as you go. Every green has a different strength, so adjust the garlic and lemon to match.

Sunflower and pumpkin seeds both work with all of these, so you can mix and match.
I got it! Junior UX designer at Fernhill Studio, starting March 2. My last shift at Lark Café is this Friday.

Congratulations, Nell! That's a big switch. For your first week: ask for the design system docs, set up one-on-ones with your manager and a buddy, sit in on a user research session if you can, and keep a list of things you don't understand yet. Nobody expects you to ship in week one.
Any advice on saying goodbye at the café?
Leave the schedule in good shape, write a short handover for whoever takes it over, and bring pastries on your last day. Café people remember that.
Can you help me write the handover for whoever takes over the schedule?

Of course. A good handover is short, scannable, and answers the questions someone will have at the worst possible moment. Here's a template you can fill in:

Schedule Handover

1. Where things live
- Where the current schedule is posted and where the master copy is kept
- Login or access details for any scheduling app (share passwords privately, not in the document)
- Where availability requests and time-off requests are collected

2. The weekly rhythm
- When the next schedule needs to be posted
- When availability is due from staff
- Any recurring deadlines, such as payroll cutoffs or supplier orders tied to staffing

3. Rules of thumb
- Minimum number of people needed for each shift
- Who is trained to open and who is trained to close
- Any shifts that are always hard to fill, and what has worked to fill them

4. Open items
- Pending time-off requests and whether they've been approved
- Shift swaps that were agreed but not yet updated
- Anything you promised someone that hasn't happened yet

5. Who to ask
- Who to go to with questions about pay, hiring, or conflicts

Keep it to one or two pages. Print a copy and leave a digital copy wherever the team normally shares things, and walk the next person through it in person if you can. Ten minutes of talking it through saves a lot of confusion later.
And a goodbye message for the team group chat?

Here are two versions, one warm and one shorter.

Version 1 (warm):
"Hi everyone! As most of you know, Friday is my last shift at Lark Café. I wanted to say thank you for making this such a good place to work. I've learned so much from all of you, from handling the morning rush to keeping a sense of humor when the grinder jams. The schedule handover is in the usual spot, and I'll walk whoever is taking it over through it before I go. I'm bringing pastries Friday, so come say hi. Please keep in touch!"

Version 2 (short):
"Hey team, Friday is my last shift. Thank you for everything; I'll miss working with you all. Handover notes are in the usual spot, and there will be pastries. Stay in touch!"

A few tips:
- Post it a few days before your last shift so people who aren't working Friday still see it.
- If there are one or two people who really helped you, a short private message to each of them means more than a mention in the group chat.
- Keep the focus on gratitude rather than on what's next. People will ask, and you can share in person.
I like the first one. Can you make it a bit less formal?

Sure, here's a looser take:

"Hey everyone! Friday's my last shift at Lark Café, which feels really strange to type. Thank you all for being the best crew. You taught me how to survive the morning rush and how to laugh when the grinder jams for the third time in an hour. Handover notes for the schedule are in the usual spot, and I'll go through them in person before I head out. Pastries are on me Friday, so swing by. Don't be strangers!"

If you want it even more casual, you could drop the line about the handover and mention it separately to the person taking over. That keeps the group message purely about saying goodbye.
Now for Fernhill. What should I ask my manager in the first one-on-one?

Your first one-on-one is mostly about understanding expectations and how your manager likes to work. Here's a list to pick from; you won't need all of them in one meeting.

Expectations
- What does a successful first month look like to you? First three months?
- What should I focus on learning first?
- Is there a starter project or a small task I can pick up to learn the process?

How the team works
- How does a project usually flow from brief to shipped design?
- Who are the people I'll work with most closely, outside the design team?
- Which tools and files should I get familiar with first?
- How are design reviews run, and when should I bring work to one?

Working with you
- How often should we meet, and what's the best way to reach you between meetings?
- Do you prefer to see work early and rough, or more polished?
- How do you like to give feedback, and how should I ask for it?

Growth
- What skills do you see as most important for someone in a junior role here?
- Are there people on the team I should learn from?

A tip: bring a notebook or a running doc, and at the end of the meeting repeat back the two or three main things you heard. It shows you were listening and clears up misunderstandings early.
What's a good way to keep that 'things I don't understand yet' list?

Keep it simple enough that you actually use it. Here's a setup that works well:

1. One running document. Use a single note or doc rather than loose sticky notes. Title it something like "Questions and notes."

2. Three sections:
- Questions: anything you don't understand yet. Jargon, acronyms, why a decision was made, how a tool works.
- Answers: when you learn the answer, copy it here with a one-line explanation in your own words. This becomes your personal glossary.
- Observations: things you notice that might be worth raising later, like a confusing flow in the product or a step in the process that seems slow. Don't act on these yet; just collect them.

3. A daily habit. Spend five minutes at the end of each day adding to it and reviewing what's open.

4. Batch your questions. Instead of interrupting people constantly, bring a few questions to your one-on-ones or to your buddy at a set time. Urgent blockers are the exception; ask those right away.

5. Try first, then ask. Before asking, spend ten or fifteen minutes looking in the docs or the design system. When you do ask, say what you already checked. People appreciate it, and you'll often get a better answer.

After a few weeks, the Answers section will be surprisingly long, and it's a nice reminder of how much you've picked up.
Any tips for the user research session if I get to sit in?

Sitting in on research is one of the best ways to learn the product and the users quickly. Some tips:

Before
- Ask the researcher if there's a discussion guide or a list of research questions you can read beforehand.
- Ask what role they'd like you to play: silent observer, note-taker, or occasional question-asker.
- Look at the part of the product being tested so you know what the participant will see.

During
- Stay quiet unless you're invited to speak. Participants get self-conscious with a crowd, and an unplanned question can lead them.
- Write down what people do, not just what they say. Hesitations, wrong clicks, and backtracking are often more telling than opinions.
- Capture direct quotes word for word when something stands out.
- Note the timestamp next to important moments so they're easy to find in the recording.
- Watch your face and body language. Avoid reacting when a participant struggles.

After
- Join the debrief if there is one. Compare notes on the biggest surprises.
- Write down your top three takeaways the same day while they're fresh.
- If something confused you about why the team asked a certain question, add it to your questions list.

One thing to remember: in research, the product is being tested, not the participant. You'll hear that said at the start of most sessions, and it's a useful mindset for reviewing your own work too.
Thanks. Can you put the first-week stuff into a simple checklist?

Here's a checklist you can copy into your notes:

Day 1
[ ] Get laptop, accounts, and tool access working
[ ] Find the design system docs and bookmark them
[ ] Set up the "Questions and notes" document
[ ] Meet your buddy and agree on a regular check-in time

Days 2 to 3
[ ] First one-on-one with your manager (bring your question list)
[ ] Read through recent project briefs or case studies
[ ] Explore the main product as a user would and jot down first impressions
[ ] Learn the file naming and organization conventions for design files

Days 4 to 5
[ ] Ask to sit in on a user research session or design review
[ ] Pick up a small starter task if one is available
[ ] Review your questions list and bring open items to your buddy
[ ] Write a short end-of-week summary: what you learned, what's still unclear, what you'd like to focus on next week

Throughout
[ ] Introduce yourself to the people you'll work with most
[ ] Take notes in meetings and repeat back key points
[ ] Ask for feedback early, even on rough work

The end-of-week summary is optional but useful. Sharing a few lines of it with your manager is an easy way to show progress and get steered in the right direction.
Can you draft a letter to my landlord? My address is 1428 Elm Street, Apt 3, Denver. The heater's broken again, third time this winter.

Here's a draft:
"Dear Mr. Alvarez, I'm writing about the heater at 1428 Elm Street, Apt 3, which stopped working on February 22. This is the third failure this winter. Please arrange a repair within 48 hours, and let me know when a technician will come. Thank you, Nell"
Keep a copy and note the date you send it.
Thanks. Also, Fernhill has an office in Boise. I might relocate at some point, so I don't want to sign a long lease.
Then ask about a month-to-month or six-month renewal. Bring it up after the heater is fixed, so the two topics don't get mixed up.
Can you make the letter a little firmer? It's not the first time.

Here's a firmer version that stays polite and sticks to facts:

"Dear Mr. Alvarez,

I'm writing to report that the heater in my apartment stopped working on February 22. This is the third heater failure this winter, and each previous repair has only been a temporary fix.

Without heat, the apartment is not livable in the current weather. I'm asking that you arrange a repair within 48 hours of receiving this letter and confirm in writing when a technician will come.

Given the repeated failures, I'd also ask that the technician assess whether the heater needs to be replaced rather than patched again, and that you share what they find.

Please reply by email or phone so we can schedule access. I'm keeping a record of this letter and of the previous repair requests.

Thank you,
Nell"

What changed and why:
- It says clearly that the problem keeps coming back, which shifts the request from a single repair to a lasting fix.
- It asks for written confirmation, which gives you a paper trail.
- It mentions that you're keeping records without sounding like a threat.

Fill in your apartment details at the top as in the first draft.
How should I send it? Email or paper?

Ideally both, and here's why:

1. Check your lease first. Many leases say how official notices should be delivered, such as in writing to a specific mailing destination or through an online portal. If there's a stated method, use it, because that's the one that counts if there's ever a dispute.

2. Email or portal message. This is fast, creates an automatic timestamp, and lets the landlord reply quickly. Attach the letter as a PDF and paste the text into the body as well.

3. Paper copy. Send a printed, signed copy by certified mail with a return receipt, or hand-deliver it and ask for a signed acknowledgment. Certified mail costs a few dollars and gives you proof of when it arrived.

4. Keep your own copies. Save the sent email, a scan of the signed letter, and the mail receipt in one folder.

If the heat is out during very cold weather, also call or text the landlord the same day so they know it's urgent. Follow up the call with a short written message like: "Just confirming our call today about the broken heater. The written request is attached." That way the phone conversation is on record too.
What should I document while I wait?

Good records make everything easier if the repair drags on. Here's what to keep:

1. A simple log. A note on your phone works. For each entry, write the date, time, and what happened:
- When the heater stopped working
- When you contacted the landlord, how, and what was said
- Any replies, scheduled visits, and whether the technician actually showed up
- What the technician did and said

2. Indoor temperature. Put a cheap thermometer in the main living area and take a photo of it with the time visible once or twice a day. This shows the real impact far better than "it's cold."

3. Photos and video. Take pictures of the heater, any error lights or messages, and the thermostat setting.

4. Past repairs. Gather whatever you have from the previous two breakdowns: emails, texts, receipts, or notes about when it was fixed.

5. Extra costs. If you buy a space heater or have higher bills because of the problem, keep the receipts. Whether you can recover them depends on local rules, but you can't ask without proof.

Store everything in one folder, digital or paper. It takes a few minutes a day and puts you in a much stronger position if you need to escalate.
What if he doesn't respond within 48 hours?

Then escalate step by step. A general outline, though tenant rules vary from place to place, so check your local ones:

1. Send a follow-up. Keep it short and factual:

"Dear Mr. Alvarez,

I'm following up on my letter about the broken heater, sent on [date]. I haven't received a response, and the apartment is still without heat. Please contact me today to arrange a repair.

Thank you,
Nell"

2. Call and leave a message, then note the time in your log.

3. Look up your local tenant rules. Many places treat heat as an essential service with specific repair timelines. Search for your local tenant rights guide, or call a local tenant hotline or legal aid office. They can tell you what remedies apply where you live.

4. Contact local housing or code enforcement. Many local housing offices will send an inspector for a lack of heat. An official inspection report carries a lot of weight.

5. Don't withhold rent on your own. In some places tenants can withhold or deduct for repairs, but only by following strict steps. Doing it wrong can put you at risk of eviction. Get advice before trying anything like that.

Most landlords respond after the first or second written request, especially when it's clear you're keeping records. The aim is to get the heat fixed, not to start a fight.
Any tips for staying warm safely in the meantime?

Yes. Safety matters most here, since a lot of winter house fires start with makeshift heating.

Space heaters
- Choose one with tip-over shutoff and overheat protection, and a safety testing mark on the label.
- Plug it directly into a wall outlet, never into an extension cord or power strip.
- Keep it at least three feet from anything that can burn: bedding, curtains, furniture, clothes.
- Turn it off when you leave the room or go to sleep.

Never use these for heat
- A gas oven or stovetop
- Outdoor grills or camp stoves
- Any fuel-burning heater not designed for indoor use
These can produce carbon monoxide. Make sure your carbon monoxide detector works, and test the smoke detectors while you're at it.

Keep the heat in
- Close doors to rooms you aren't using and heat the one you're in.
- Hang heavy curtains or a blanket over drafty windows at night, and open them during sunny days.
- Roll a towel along the bottom of doors to block drafts.

Keep yourself warm
- Layers, warm socks, and a hat do more than you'd expect.
- Flannel sheets and an extra blanket make nights much more comfortable.
- Warm drinks and regular meals help your body generate heat.

If the indoor temperature falls very low, or pipes are at risk of freezing, tell the landlord that too. Frozen pipes are expensive for them, which can speed up a response.
Once the heater's fixed, can you draft the email about lease terms?

Sure. Here's a draft that keeps it friendly and separate from the repair issue:

Subject: Lease renewal options

"Dear Mr. Alvarez,

Thank you for getting the heater repaired. I appreciate it.

When it's time to renew my lease, I'd like to understand my options. Because there's a chance I may relocate in the next year or so, I'd prefer a shorter term rather than another twelve-month lease. Would you be open to a month-to-month arrangement or a six-month renewal?

I understand shorter terms sometimes come with a different rent. Could you let me know what each option would cost and any other terms that would change?

I've been glad to live here and would like to stay on a flexible basis. Thanks for considering it.

Best regards,
Nell"

Why this works:
- Opening with thanks sets a positive tone after the repair.
- It gives a reason without oversharing.
- Asking for the cost of each option lets you compare instead of accepting the first offer.
- It signals you're a tenant who wants to stay, which landlords value.

Send it well before your renewal deadline. Your lease should say how much notice is needed.
What if he only offers a 12-month lease?

That's common, so it helps to have a plan. A few options to explore:

1. Ask about the early termination terms. Read the lease for a clause about breaking it early. Some leases allow it with a set fee, often one or two months' rent, plus a notice period. If that cost is manageable, a twelve-month lease may be fine.

2. Negotiate an early termination clause. If there isn't one, ask to add it. For example: "Tenant may end the lease early with 60 days' written notice and a fee equal to one month's rent." Landlords often agree because it gives them certainty.

3. Ask about subletting or lease assignment. If you leave early, being allowed to find a replacement tenant can reduce or eliminate penalties. Get any permission in writing.
