4. Compare costs. If month-to-month is offered at a higher rent, work out the total over a year and compare it with the twelve-month rent plus a possible early termination fee. Sometimes the longer lease with an exit clause is cheaper even if you leave early.

5. Check local rules. Some places require landlords to make a reasonable effort to re-rent the unit if a tenant leaves early, which limits what you'd owe. A tenant hotline can tell you how it works where you are.

Whatever you agree on, make sure the final terms are written into the lease or an addendum signed by both of you, not just mentioned in an email or conversation.
First week at Fernhill went well! Everyone's nice. Also, Biscuit has a sister now: we adopted a terrier mix named Pepper.

That's a big week! To introduce them: walk them together on neutral ground first, feed them in separate spots, and give each one some time alone with you. Terriers can be bossy, so watch for guarding around toys and beds.
Pepper already stole Biscuit's bed.
Classic terrier. Get a second bed and praise them both for settling on their own.
Should the second bed go right next to the first one?

Not right next to it at first. Give each dog a bit of space so neither feels crowded. Some guidelines:

1. Separate but visible. Put the beds in the same room, a few feet apart, so both dogs can see each other and you. Dogs like to be near the group, but they also like a spot that's clearly their own.

2. Pick quiet corners. Avoid doorways and hallways where one dog has to walk past the other to get somewhere. Tight spots are where squabbles start.

3. Make both beds equally appealing. If one bed is clearly better (softer, warmer, closer to you), both dogs will want it. Similar beds in similar spots reduce competition.

4. Use the old bed's smell. Biscuit's original bed already smells familiar, which is part of why Pepper wants it. You can rub a towel on Biscuit and put it in the new bed, or simply let Pepper keep the old one if Biscuit doesn't mind and give Biscuit the new one with the familiar blanket.

5. Reward the right choice. When each dog lies down on their own bed, calmly praise them or drop a treat between their paws.

Once they're comfortable with each other, many dogs end up sharing a bed or sleeping side by side on their own. Let that happen naturally rather than forcing it.
How do I tell if they're playing or actually fighting?

It can look and sound alarming, but play and fighting have pretty clear differences once you know what to look for.

Signs of healthy play
- Loose, wiggly bodies and relaxed faces, often with open mouths
- Play bows: front end down, rear end up
- Taking turns: one chases, then the other; one is on top, then the other
- Self-handicapping: the bigger or stronger dog holds back
- Exaggerated, bouncy motions
- Short breaks where they shake off, sniff around, then start again
- Growling that sounds noisy but loose

Warning signs
- Stiff, frozen bodies or a hard stare
- One dog always on top or always chasing, with no switching
- Hackles up along the whole back, ears pinned flat, lips pulled tight
- One dog trying to escape, hiding, or tucking the tail while the other keeps going
- Growls that are low and steady rather than playful
- Yelps that don't lead to a pause

A simple test
If you're unsure, gently separate them for a few seconds by calling one away. If the other dog follows and invites more play, they're both having fun. If that dog takes the chance to leave, they wanted a break.

When to step in
Interrupt early, before things escalate. Call one dog away cheerfully, toss a treat, and give them a minute apart. Never reach between dogs that are actually fighting; use a loud noise or put a cushion between them instead.
What about toys? Pepper keeps taking Biscuit's.

That's very common with a new terrier. Some practical steps:

1. Pick up the high-value toys for now. Keep favorite toys, chews, and anything they fight over put away when you aren't actively supervising. Leave out only boring, low-value toys that neither cares much about.

2. Separate time for good stuff. Give special chews and favorite toys when the dogs are in different rooms or crates. Each gets to enjoy their own without having to defend it.

3. Have plenty to go around. When toys are out, put out more than two, so there's always something else to grab.

4. Teach "drop it" and "leave it." Practice with each dog separately first, trading the toy for a treat. Once they're reliable, you can use these cues to stop a toy grab before it starts.

5. Watch for guarding signals. Freezing over a toy, hard staring, lip lifting, or growling when the other dog approaches are signs of resource guarding. Calmly call the approaching dog away rather than scolding the one that's guarding. Punishing the warning can make dogs skip the warning next time.

6. Don't let one dog bully. If Pepper is taking toys out of Biscuit's mouth, calmly interrupt and redirect Pepper to another toy. Biscuit should get to keep the toy.

Most toy squabbles settle down within a few weeks as the dogs work out their relationship, especially if you prevent constant conflicts in the meantime. If guarding gets more intense or anyone gets hurt, a certified trainer or behaviorist is worth calling.
Can you explain the feeding setup in more detail?

Sure. Mealtimes are one of the most common flash points between dogs, so a clear routine helps a lot.

1. Separate spots. Feed them in different rooms, or at least on opposite sides of a room with a barrier between them. Each dog should be able to eat without seeing the other one staring.

2. Same order, same time. Prepare both bowls, then put them down in the same order every meal. Predictability lowers stress.

3. Wait for calm. Ask each dog to sit or wait before the bowl goes down. This keeps excitement low.

4. Supervise. Stay nearby until both have finished. Fast eaters often finish first and then wander over to the other bowl.

5. Pick up the bowls. As soon as each dog is done, pick up that bowl, even if it's empty. Empty bowls can still be guarded, and leftover food invites trouble.

6. Slow down a fast eater. If one dog inhales food, try a slow-feeder bowl or a puzzle feeder. It gives her something to do and makes it less likely to hover around the other dog.

7. Use crates or gates if needed. Feeding each dog in a separate crate is an easy way to keep meals completely separate.

Treats work the same way: hand them out one at a time to each dog, using names, and have both dogs sit a few feet apart. Once they're used to each other, you can gradually relax the setup, but many households keep separate feeding spots forever because it's simple and peaceful.
How long until they're actually settled with each other?

It varies a lot, but a common rule of thumb is the "3-3-3" guideline for a new dog:

- First 3 days: The new dog is often overloaded. She may be quiet, unsure, or a bit wild. Don't read too much into her behavior yet.
- First 3 weeks: She starts learning the routine and the house rules. Her real personality begins to show, and so do any conflicts with the resident dog.
- First 3 months: She feels at home. Most relationships between dogs settle into a pattern by this point.

For the two dogs specifically, many households see a noticeable improvement within a few weeks, with a fully settled relationship taking a few months. A few things affect the timeline:

1. Structure. A consistent routine for walks, meals, and rest helps both dogs relax faster.
2. Space. Giving each dog time alone, and time alone with you, prevents a lot of tension.
3. Prevention. Managing toys, food, and beds keeps small problems from becoming habits.
4. Personality. Some pairs click immediately; others take longer to work out who gets what.

Good signs that things are going well:
- They relax and nap in the same room
- Play is balanced and they take breaks
- They greet each other calmly after time apart
- Squabbles are brief and end without lasting tension

If after a few months there's still frequent growling, hard stares, or actual fights, a professional trainer can help you work out what's driving it.
Any tips for walking them together? Pepper pulls a lot.

Walking two dogs is much easier once each one walks reasonably well alone. Some steps:

1. Train separately first. Spend a few short walks working with Pepper on her own. Every time the leash tightens, stop and stand still. When she comes back or the leash loosens, praise her and keep walking. It's slow at first, but she'll learn that pulling doesn't get her anywhere.

2. Reward a loose leash. Carry small treats and reward her for walking next to you. Many dogs pull because sniffing and moving forward are their reward, so you need to offer something better.

3. Consider a front-clip harness. A harness with the leash attached at the chest turns a pulling dog sideways, which takes the power out of the pull. It's gentler than a collar and often makes a big difference quickly.

4. Use two separate leashes. Avoid coupler leashes that join both dogs on one handle. Separate leashes give you more control and stop one dog from dragging the other.

5. Keep them on fixed sides. Have one dog always on your left and the other always on your right. It cuts down on tangling and gives each dog a predictable spot.

6. Start short and quiet. Practice walking them together on short, quiet routes before trying busy areas or new places.

7. Let them sniff. Build in short sniff breaks on a cue like "go sniff." Sniffing is mentally tiring for dogs, and a tired dog pulls less.

Terriers are often energetic and determined, so give Pepper plenty of chances to burn energy with play and puzzle toys as well. A dog with energy left over will put it into the leash.
That's helpful. Can you sum it all up as a quick daily routine?

Here's a simple daily routine based on everything above. Adjust the times to whatever fits your day.

Morning
- Short walk: each dog on a separate leash and a set side. Practice loose-leash walking with Pepper.
- Breakfast: separate spots, same order, bowls picked up when done.
- Calm time: both dogs on their own beds with a low-value chew or toy.

Midday
- If possible, a potty break and a short sniff walk.
- Puzzle feeder or chew in separate spaces if they're left alone. Put away favorite toys before you leave.

Evening
- Longer walk or play session to burn energy. Watch play for balance and breaks.
- A few minutes of training each: "drop it," "leave it," and settling on a bed.
- Dinner: same setup as breakfast.

Before bed
- Short potty walk.
- Each dog on their own bed, with praise for settling.

Throughout the day
- One-on-one time with each dog, even ten minutes.
- Interrupt rough play early and give short breaks apart.
- High-value toys only when supervised or separated.

Weekly check-in
- Are they napping closer together? Fewer squabbles over toys? More relaxed at meals?

Keep the routine consistent for the next few weeks, then relax things gradually as they settle. Small, steady progress is what you're looking for.
I signed up for the Boise half marathon on May 9. I've never run more than 10K. Is eight weeks enough?

It's tight but doable from a 10K base. Run three times a week: one easy run, one with short intervals, and a long run that grows about a mile a week to 10 or 11 miles two weeks out. Then taper. Most important: keep the easy days truly easy.
A coworker from the Boise office talked me into it. Can you write the week-by-week plan?

Week 1: easy 3 mi, intervals 6×400 m, long 5 mi
Week 2: easy 3, intervals 6×400, long 6
Week 3: easy 4, tempo 2 mi, long 7
Week 4: easy 3, intervals 8×400, long 8
Week 5: easy 4, tempo 3, long 9
Week 6: easy 4, intervals 6×800, long 10–11
Week 7: easy 3, tempo 2, long 7
Week 8: two short easy runs, then race day
How fast should the easy runs be?

Slower than most people think. Easy runs build your aerobic base, help you recover, and add mileage without wearing you down. Here are three ways to check you're going easy enough:

1. The talk test. You should be able to speak in full sentences without gasping. If you can only manage a few words at a time, slow down.

2. Effort scale. On a scale of 1 to 10, where 10 is an all-out sprint, easy runs should feel like a 3 or 4. Comfortable, almost lazy.

3. Pace relative to your 10K. A common guideline is to run easy days about 1 to 2 minutes per mile slower than your 10K race pace. If that feels absurdly slow, that's normal; it's supposed to.

If you use a heart rate monitor, easy runs typically fall around 65 to 75 percent of maximum heart rate. Wrist-based monitors can be unreliable, though, so trust the talk test over the number if they disagree.

Take walk breaks on hills or when your breathing climbs; that's completely fine on easy days. The hard work happens in the interval and tempo sessions. If you run your easy days too fast, you'll be too tired to get the most out of those.
And how do I do the intervals? I've never done 400s.

400 meters is one lap of a standard outdoor track, so a track is the easiest place to do them. Here's how a session works:

1. Warm up. Jog easily for 10 to 15 minutes. Then do a few dynamic drills (leg swings, high knees, butt kicks) and two or three strides: 20-second pickups where you gradually speed up to a fast but relaxed pace, then walk back.

2. The repeats. Run 400 meters at a hard but controlled effort, about an 8 out of 10. For a target, aim for roughly your 5K race pace, or a little faster than 10K pace. You should finish each one feeling like you could do a couple more.

3. Recovery. After each repeat, walk or jog slowly for about 200 meters, or 90 seconds to 2 minutes. Let your breathing settle before the next one.

4. Consistency. Try to run every repeat at about the same time. If the last ones are much slower than the first, you started too fast. Better to finish strong than fade.

5. Cool down. Jog easily for 10 minutes, then walk.

No track? Use a flat stretch of road or path and run for about 90 seconds to 2 minutes hard instead of measuring distance. A GPS watch or phone app can also mark 400 meters for you.

The 800s in week 6 work the same way, just twice as long, with about 2 to 3 minutes of recovery between them. Run them a little slower than the 400s.
What's a tempo run exactly?

A tempo run is a sustained effort at a "comfortably hard" pace. It trains your body to hold a faster pace for longer before fatigue builds up, which is exactly what you need for a half marathon.

How it should feel
- About a 6 or 7 out of 10 effort
- You can say a few words, but not hold a conversation
- Hard enough to require focus, but steady, not a sprint
- Roughly the pace you could hold for about an hour in a race; for many runners that's somewhere between 10K pace and half marathon pace

How to structure it
1. Warm up with 10 to 15 minutes of easy running.
2. Run the tempo portion at a steady pace. In your plan, that's 2 miles in week 3, 3 miles in week 5, and 2 miles in week 7.
3. Cool down with 10 minutes of easy running.

Common mistakes
- Starting too fast. Tempo runs should be even. If you're struggling badly in the last half mile, slow down next time.
- Turning it into a race. Hard is not the goal; steady is.
- Skipping the warm-up. Jumping straight into tempo pace feels awful and raises injury risk.

If holding the full distance is too much at first, split it: for example, two 1-mile segments with a 2-minute easy jog in between. That still gives you most of the benefit.
Do I need to eat anything during the long runs?

For runs under about an hour, most people don't need anything except water. Once your long runs pass 60 to 75 minutes, which will happen around weeks 4 to 6, it's worth practicing fueling. Here's how to approach it:

Before the run
- Eat a light, carb-focused snack 1 to 2 hours before: toast with jam, a banana, oatmeal, or a bagel.
- Avoid a lot of fat, fiber, or anything new right before a long run.
- Drink water, but don't overdo it right before you start.

During the run
- Aim for about 30 to 60 grams of carbohydrate per hour once you're past an hour. Energy gels, chews, sports drinks, or even dried fruit all work.
- Start fueling around 45 minutes in, then take something every 30 to 45 minutes.
- Take gels with water, not sports drink, to avoid stomach upset.
- Sip water regularly, especially in warm weather. Drink to thirst rather than forcing it.

After the run
- Eat a meal or snack with carbohydrates and protein within an hour or so. Chocolate milk, a sandwich, or eggs and toast all work.
- Rehydrate over the next few hours.

The most important rule: practice on your long runs exactly what you plan to do on race day. Find out which gels or snacks your stomach tolerates now, not at mile 9 of the race. Many races list which brand of sports drink or gel they'll hand out on the course, so it's worth training with that if you can.
What if I miss a run or feel sore?

Both happen to almost everyone, and handling them well matters more than following the plan perfectly.

Missing a run
- Missed one easy run: just skip it. Don't try to cram it in later.
- Missed the interval or tempo session: if you can fit it in the next day and still have a rest day before the long run, do it. Otherwise skip it.
- Missed the long run: this is the most important session of the week. Shift other runs around to fit it in if you can, as long as you leave a day between hard efforts.
- Missed a whole week (illness or life getting busy): repeat the previous week rather than jumping ahead, and accept a slightly shorter longest run. Arriving healthy matters more than hitting every mile.

General soreness
Muscle soreness a day or two after a hard run is normal, especially when your long runs reach new distances. To help:
- Keep the next run truly easy, or swap it for a walk.
- Gentle stretching, foam rolling, and staying active help more than complete rest.
- Sleep and eating enough are the most effective recovery tools there are.

When to stop and rest
Soreness that's general, spread across a muscle, and fades as you warm up is usually fine. These are warning signs:
- Sharp or localized pain, especially in a bone or joint
- Pain that gets worse as you run
- Pain that makes you limp or change your stride
- Swelling, or pain that lingers for more than a few days

If you notice any of those, stop running for a few days and see a doctor or physical therapist if it doesn't improve. Taking a few days off now is far better than missing weeks with an injury.
Can you explain the taper? Week 7 and 8 look really light.

That's on purpose. The taper is when you cut back so your body can recover and absorb the training you've done. You don't gain much fitness in the last two weeks, but you can lose a lot of freshness by running too much.

What happens during a taper
- Muscles repair the small damage from training.
- Energy stores in your muscles fill back up.
- Accumulated fatigue fades, so you start the race feeling springy instead of heavy.

How your plan does it
- Week 7: your long run drops from 10 or 11 miles back to 7, and the tempo shortens to 2 miles. You still run three times, with some quality, but less total volume.
- Week 8: just two short easy runs before race day. Adding a few 20-second strides at the end of one of them keeps your legs feeling sharp.

What to expect
Many runners feel restless, sluggish, or oddly achy during the taper. It's often called "taper madness," and it's normal. Resist the urge to squeeze in an extra run to prove you're still fit. You are.

The last few days
- Keep your routine familiar.
- Prioritize sleep, especially two nights before the race, since nerves often disrupt the night right before.
- Eat normal meals with a bit more carbohydrate the day before. You don't need to stuff yourself.
- Don't try new shoes, new foods, or a new gel.

Trust the training. By week 7, the hard work is already done.
And a race-day checklist?

Here's a checklist split into the night before, the morning of, and the race itself.

The night before
[ ] Lay out your outfit, the one you've already tested on long runs
[ ] Pin your bib to your shirt or a race belt
[ ] Charge your watch and phone
[ ] Pack gels or chews, plus any body glide or anti-chafe balm
[ ] Plan how you'll get to the start and when you need to leave
[ ] Eat a familiar dinner and drink water through the evening
[ ] Set two alarms

The morning of
[ ] Eat your usual pre-run breakfast 2 to 3 hours before the start
[ ] Sip water, but don't overdo it
[ ] Dress for the weather a few degrees warmer than it feels; you'll heat up fast
[ ] Wear an old layer to the start that you can toss or check
[ ] Arrive early enough for the bathroom line, which is always long
[ ] Do a short warm-up: 5 to 10 minutes of easy jogging and a few strides

During the race
[ ] Start slower than you want to. The first mile should feel easy.
[ ] Settle into a steady effort for miles 2 to 8
[ ] Take fuel on the schedule you practiced
[ ] Walk through aid stations if it helps you drink
[ ] If you feel good at mile 10, pick it up a little
[ ] Smile at the finish for the photo

Afterward
[ ] Keep walking for a few minutes; don't sit down right away
[ ] Drink, eat something with carbs and protein, and change into dry clothes
[ ] Take a few easy days before running again

For a first half marathon, the best goal is to finish feeling strong. A conservative start almost always pays off in the second half.
We moved to Boise this weekend! Sold my bike, it didn't fit in the truck.

Welcome to Boise! First-week checklist: set up utilities and internet, update your address with the post office and your bank, get an Idaho driver's license within 90 days, license the dogs with the city, and find a vet. The Boise River Greenbelt is great for dog walks.
The dogs already love the Greenbelt.
Perfect. Their noses will be busy for weeks.
Can you help me plan the unpacking? There are boxes everywhere and I'm not sure where to start.

Sure. The trick is to unpack in the order you need things to live day to day, not room by room in whatever order the boxes landed. Here's a plan that works for most people:

Day 1: the survival layer
- Beds first. Assemble the frames, or at least get the mattresses down and make them up with clean sheets. A good night's sleep matters more than anything else this week.
- Bathroom basics: towels, toilet paper, soap, toothbrushes, a shower curtain, and any daily prescriptions.
- Dog setup: food and water bowls, food, leashes, poop bags, and their beds or blankets. Familiar-smelling bedding helps them feel at home faster.
- A few kitchen essentials: one pan, one pot, a knife, a cutting board, a couple of plates and bowls, mugs, and the coffee or tea setup.

Days 2 and 3: the kitchen
The kitchen has the most items and the most decisions, so give it a full block of time. Unpack in this order: everyday dishes and utensils, pantry staples, cookware, then small appliances. Leave rarely used items (serving platters, specialty gadgets, seasonal baking gear) in their boxes and stash those boxes in a closet to sort later.

Days 4 and 5: bedroom and clothes
Hang what you wear most, fold the rest, and don't worry about organizing drawers perfectly. Good enough is fine for now.

Week 2: living areas, books, decor, and any storage boxes.

A few tips that speed things up:
- Break down boxes as you empty them and stack them flat by the door. Visible progress is motivating, and it clears floor space.
- Keep one open 'misc' box per room for things that don't have a home yet, instead of letting them spread across counters.
- Work in 45-minute stretches with a 15-minute break. Long unbroken sessions lead to burnout by day three.
That helps. Can you expand the change-of-address list? I keep remembering places I forgot.

Here's a fuller list, grouped so you can work through it in one or two sittings. Most of these take a few minutes each online.

Official
- USPS mail forwarding, if it isn't set up yet. Forwarding can run up to a year, but update senders directly so you aren't relying on it.
- IRS: you can file Form 8822, or simply use the new address on your next return.
- Voter registration for Idaho.
- Any professional licenses or memberships that mail renewals.

Money
- Banks and credit unions
- Credit cards (the billing ZIP code is often used to verify card purchases, so update it early to avoid declined payments)
- Investment and retirement accounts
- Payment apps like PayPal or Venmo
- Any loan servicers

Insurance
- Health insurance (your plan's network may differ in a new state, so check that too)
- Renters or homeowners insurance
- Life insurance
- Pet insurance, if the dogs have it

Health
- Doctor and dentist (or request records to be sent to new ones)
- Pharmacy: transfer prescriptions to a local branch
- Eye doctor

Shopping and subscriptions
- Default shipping info on Amazon and other retailers. This is the one people forget most, and packages end up at the old place.
- Meal kits, subscription boxes, and pet food deliveries
- Streaming services and phone carrier (billing info)

The dogs
- Microchip registry. It's easy to overlook, and it's what a shelter uses to reach you if one of them gets loose.
- ID tags with a current phone number
- Vet records and the city dog license

A useful habit: over the next couple of months, glance at every piece of forwarded mail. Anything that arrives through forwarding is a sender you missed, so update it right then.
What should I look for when choosing a vet for the dogs?

Good thing to sort out before you need one. Here's what to weigh:

Practical basics
- Distance. Close enough that a quick visit is easy, since you'll be there more often than you expect.
- Hours. Ask whether they offer early morning, evening, or Saturday appointments.
- Emergency coverage. Ask what they do after hours. Most general clinics refer to a 24-hour emergency hospital, so find out which one and save its number in your phone now.
- Booking. How far out are routine appointments booked? Can you get a same-day sick visit?

Care and conversation
- Do the vets explain options and costs before treating, or just proceed?
- Do they send estimates in writing for anything beyond a routine exam?
- Is there a patient portal for records, reminders, and messaging?
- Are they open to questions about food, behavior, and preventive care, or do visits feel rushed?

Credentials and setup
- AAHA accreditation is a voluntary standard that covers things like anesthesia monitoring, sterilization, and record keeping. Not every good clinic has it, but it's a positive sign.
- Fear Free certified staff can make visits less stressful for anxious dogs.
- Ask whether they do dental cleanings, X-rays, and bloodwork in-house or send you elsewhere.

How to find candidates
- Ask neighbors you meet on walks. Dog owners on the Greenbelt are usually happy to share opinions.
- Read recent reviews, focusing on how the clinic handled problems rather than star ratings alone.
- Call two or three clinics and ask about new-patient availability and exam fees. How the front desk treats you on the phone tells you a lot.

Once you pick one, book a wellness visit for each dog while they're healthy. It sets a baseline, gets them into the system, and makes a future sick visit much faster to arrange.
How do I get their records sent over from the old vet?

It's usually quick. Here's the process:

1. Call or email the old clinic and ask for the complete medical records for each dog, not just the vaccine summary. Full records include exam notes, lab results, past prescriptions, and any surgeries or dental work.
2. Ask them to email the records as PDFs to you, and also send them straight to the new clinic once you've chosen one. Having your own copy means you're never stuck waiting on a fax.
3. Request proof of current rabies vaccination for each dog. Most cities, including Boise, ask for it when you license a dog, so you'll want it handy.
4. Write down each dog's microchip number and the registry company. It's often in the records, but double-check.
5. Note any prescriptions, doses, and refill dates so the new vet can take over prescriptions without a gap.

Store everything in one folder on your phone or in cloud storage, named clearly by dog. When the new clinic sends its intake form, you can attach the files and be done in a few minutes.

If the old clinic is slow, a polite follow-up after a few days usually does it. Clinics handle these requests constantly.
Any tips for helping dogs settle into a new home?

Yes, a few things make a real difference:

Keep the routine steady
Dogs take a lot of comfort from predictability. Feed them, walk them, and settle them for bed at the same times you always have. When the house is unfamiliar, the schedule becomes their anchor.

Set up their space first
Put their beds, bowls, and toys in spots that will stay put, so they learn where 'their' places are. Don't wash their bedding for the first week or two; the familiar smell is reassuring.

Explore gradually
Let them sniff the house room by room with you nearby. Close off any rooms with unpacked boxes, cords, or cleaning supplies until those areas are sorted.

Check the yard and doors
Walk the fence line, if there is one, and look for gaps or loose boards. In a new place, dogs are more likely to bolt if a door is left open, so be extra careful during the unpacking chaos when people are coming and going.

Burn off energy
Long sniffy walks are calming because sniffing is mentally tiring. The Greenbelt is ideal for that. A tired dog adapts faster.

Expect a little adjustment
Some dogs are restless at night, bark at new sounds, or have a small accident in the first week or two. That's normal. Stay calm, keep the routine, and it usually fades on its own. If anything persists past a few weeks, mention it at the first vet visit.

Update their tags
If it's not done yet, put a phone number on their collars today. It's the single most important safety step during a transition.
And for utilities and internet, anything I should double-check?

A few things worth confirming now so there are no surprises on the first bills:

- Start dates. Make sure each service is in your name starting on the day you took possession, and that the old place's accounts are closed so you're not paying for both.
- Providers. In Boise, electricity is generally Idaho Power and natural gas is usually Intermountain Gas. Water and trash can vary by neighborhood, so confirm who serves your home.
- Deposits. Some utilities waive the deposit if you have a good payment history or a letter of credit from your previous provider. It's worth asking.
- Trash and recycling. Find out your pickup day and what goes in which bin. Recycling rules differ a lot between cities, so check the current list rather than assuming.
- Internet. Confirm the speed you're actually getting with a quick speed test, and compare it to what you're paying for. If it's far lower, call support early while the install is fresh.
- Router placement. Put the router in a central, open spot, off the floor and away from the microwave. Change the default Wi-Fi name and password, and the router's admin password too.
- Autopay and paperless billing. Set these up once you've seen the first bill and know it's correct.
- Meter readings. Take photos of the meters on day one. If there's ever a billing dispute, you have a timestamped starting point.
Last one: a simple meal plan for this week while most of the kitchen is still in boxes?

Here's a low-effort plan that needs only one pan, one pot, and a sheet tray:

Breakfasts (rotate)
- Overnight oats in jars: oats, milk or yogurt, fruit. Make three at once.
- Toast with eggs or avocado.
- Yogurt, granola, and fruit when you're short on time.

Lunches
- Wraps with rotisserie chicken, greens, and hummus.
- Leftovers from the previous dinner.
- A big grain salad made on Sunday: cooked rice or farro, canned beans, chopped vegetables, olive oil, and lemon. It keeps for four days.

Dinners
- Night 1: sheet-pan sausage and vegetables. Toss everything with oil and salt, roast at 425°F for about 25 minutes.
- Night 2: pasta with jarred sauce, a bag of spinach stirred in, and parmesan.
- Night 3: tacos with rotisserie chicken or canned black beans, salsa, and shredded cabbage.
- Night 4: fried rice with frozen vegetables and eggs. Uses up leftover rice.
- Night 5: takeout. You've earned it, and it's a good way to try a local spot.
- Night 6: quesadillas and a bagged salad kit.
- Night 7: soup from a carton, upgraded with frozen dumplings or tortellini, and toast.

Shopping list basics
Rotisserie chicken, eggs, bread, tortillas, a carton of soup, pasta, jarred sauce, rice, canned beans, frozen vegetables, a bag of spinach, salad kit, cheese, salsa, hummus, yogurt, fruit, oats, olive oil, salt.

A couple of tips: use paper plates for the first few days if the dishwasher isn't hooked up yet, and keep a roll of foil on hand so the sheet tray needs almost no cleanup. Once the kitchen is unpacked, you can go back to cooking the way you like.
Now I drive to the Fernhill office here in Boise, about 35 minutes each way. Podcast ideas for the drive?
35 minutes is a nice length. For design: Design Better and 99% Invisible. For running: Marathon Training Academy. Just for fun: Radiolab. Episodes of 30 to 40 minutes fit one leg of the drive.
Can you suggest a few more in different genres? I'd like some variety across the week.

Absolutely. Here's a spread across genres, with typical episode lengths, since that matters for a 35-minute drive.

Storytelling
- This American Life: about an hour, but it's split into acts, so it breaks naturally across two trips.
- The Moth: true stories told live on stage. Episodes run around 50 minutes, but each story is 10 to 15 minutes, so stopping mid-episode is painless.
- Heavyweight: the host helps people revisit an unresolved moment from their past. Usually 30 to 45 minutes and very well produced.

Science and ideas
- Hidden Brain: psychology and human behavior, usually 45 to 55 minutes.
- Science Vs: takes a popular claim and checks it against the research. Around 30 to 40 minutes.
- Ologies: long conversations with researchers about one specialty each. Often over an hour, so better for listening in pieces.

History
- Revisionist History: Malcolm Gladwell revisits overlooked events and ideas. Usually 35 to 45 minutes.
- You're Dead to Me: a historian and a comedian cover one topic per episode. Fun and easy to follow.

News
- The Daily: about 25 to 30 minutes on one story in depth. A good fit for the morning leg.
- Up First: around 15 minutes of headlines when you want something shorter.

Lighter listening
- Wait Wait... Don't Tell Me!: the weekly news quiz show, about 50 minutes.
- Conan O'Brien Needs a Friend: long-form comedy conversations.

More on your existing interests
- Design Matters with Debbie Millman: long interviews with artists and creative leaders about their careers and process.
- The Morning Shakeout: conversations about running and training, a nice companion to Marathon Training Academy.

You don't need all of these. Pick three or four to subscribe to and keep the rest as a backup list for when you get bored.
Could you turn that into a weekly rotation?

Here's a simple rotation that keeps things varied without requiring decisions every morning. Mornings lean toward shorter, focused shows to start the day; evenings lean toward stories and lighter listening for winding down.

Monday
- Morning: The Daily
- Evening: Design Better

Tuesday
- Morning: Science Vs
- Evening: The Moth (two or three stories)

Wednesday
- Morning: The Daily
- Evening: Marathon Training Academy

Thursday
- Morning: Hidden Brain (first part)
- Evening: Hidden Brain (finish), then whatever's left of the drive with Up First

Friday
- Morning: Revisionist History
- Evening: Wait Wait... Don't Tell Me! or a comedy show to kick off the weekend

A few rules that keep the system from turning into a chore:
- Flex slot. Treat Friday evening as a free pick. If something in your queue looks more interesting, play that instead.
- Backlog cap. Don't let more than five unplayed episodes pile up per show. If a show keeps piling up, it's probably not one you actually want; unsubscribe without guilt.
- Skip freely. If an episode isn't grabbing you in the first five minutes, skip it. There's always another one.
- Seasonal swaps. Every month or so, rotate one show out and try something from the backup list. It keeps the drive feeling fresh.

If you prefer, you can also go by mood instead of by day: one 'learning' show in the morning and one 'fun' show in the evening, choosing from a short list for each. Some people find that less rigid and easier to stick with.
How do I set up my podcast app so the next episode just plays without me touching the phone?

Good idea, since fiddling with the phone while driving is exactly what you want to avoid. The goal is a ready-made queue that plays in order. Here's how to set it up in the most common apps:

Apple Podcasts
1. Open an episode, tap the three-dot menu, and choose Play Next or Play Last to build your Up Next queue.
2. In Settings > Apps > Podcasts, turn on Continuous Playback so it rolls into the next episode automatically.
3. Turn on automatic downloads for the shows you follow, so episodes are stored on the phone and don't depend on cell signal.

Pocket Casts
1. Use the Up Next queue; long-press an episode to add it to the top or bottom.
2. Under Settings > Auto Add to Up Next, choose which shows are added automatically when a new episode drops.
3. Set auto-download to Wi-Fi only to save mobile data.

Spotify
1. Tap the three dots on an episode and choose Add to Queue.
2. Turn on Autoplay in settings, although for podcasts it sometimes plays related episodes rather than your queue, so building the queue manually is more reliable.
3. Download episodes you plan to hear on the road.

In the car
- If your car supports CarPlay or Android Auto, the queue shows up on the dashboard screen, and you can skip with the steering wheel buttons.
- Voice commands work well for basics: 'Hey Siri, play my podcasts' or 'Hey Google, play the next episode.'
- Turn on your phone's Driving Focus (iPhone) or Driving Mode (Android) to silence alerts and texts.

The five-minute habit
Build the next day's queue the evening before, while you're parked or at home. Then you just start the car, press play once, and the drive takes care of itself.
What if an episode runs longer than the drive?

That's fine, and most apps handle it well. A few approaches:

- Let it resume. Every major podcast app remembers your position, so a 60-minute episode just becomes the morning and evening listen. This works best for interview shows and storytelling shows with natural breaks.
- Speed it up a little. Many people find 1.2x to 1.3x sounds natural after a few days. At 1.25x, a 45-minute episode fits in 36 minutes, almost exactly one trip.
- Trim silence. Pocket Casts has Trim Silence, and Overcast has Smart Speed. Both shorten pauses without making voices sound rushed and can save several minutes per hour.
- Use chapters. Some shows include chapter markers, so you can stop at a clean break instead of mid-sentence.
- Match by length. Put longer episodes on days when you know you'll want to continue, and keep shorter ones for days you'd rather start fresh each trip.

One tip: if you stop mid-episode for more than a day or two, rewind 30 seconds when you restart. It's much easier to pick up the thread.
Are audiobooks worth trying too?

Definitely. A 35-minute drive each way adds up to almost six hours a week, which is enough to finish a typical audiobook in a week or two.

Where to get them
- Libby: free with a public library card. Popular titles can have wait lists, so place holds on several books at once.
- Libro.fm: a paid membership with one credit a month, and part of each purchase supports an independent bookstore of your choice.
- Audible: the largest selection, also credit-based, and often has sales.
- Spotify: some plans include a set number of audiobook hours per month.

What works well while driving
- Narrative nonfiction and memoirs, especially ones read by the author.
- Thrillers and fast-paced fiction with a small cast, so you don't lose track of who's who.
- Books with short chapters, which give you natural stopping points.

What's harder
- Dense nonfiction with lots of charts or numbers.
- Fiction with a huge cast or frequent time jumps.

A few well-loved picks to try
- Project Hail Mary by Andy Weir, narrated by Ray Porter: funny, tense, and great on audio.
- Born a Crime by Trevor Noah, read by the author.
- The Martian, also by Andy Weir.
- Shoe Dog by Phil Knight, a readable business memoir.

You could also slot an audiobook into the rotation on one or two days a week and keep podcasts for the rest.
Any tips for remembering more of what I listen to?

Yes. Most of what you hear on the road fades quickly unless you do something with it, but a tiny bit of effort helps a lot:

- One-sentence summary. When you park, take 30 seconds to say or type the one idea you want to keep. A voice memo is fastest. This is the single most effective habit.
- Bookmarks and clips. Apps like Snipd and Airr let you save a clip with one tap, and Pocket Casts lets you add bookmarks. Use the headphone or steering wheel controls if they're set up, and only tap the screen when you're stopped.
- Weekly review. On the weekend, skim your notes or clips for five minutes. Revisiting an idea a few days later is what pushes it into long-term memory.
- Talk about it. Explaining an idea from an episode to someone else is a great memory aid.
- Fewer, better. Listening to fewer shows with more attention beats skimming many.

And don't worry about remembering everything. Some episodes are just good company for the drive, and that's a perfectly fine reason to listen.
Can you recap the whole setup as a short checklist?

Here you go:

Setup (once)
- Subscribe to three or four core shows plus a short backup list.
- Turn on auto-download over Wi-Fi.
- Turn on continuous playback.
- Connect CarPlay or Android Auto if available.
- Turn on Driving Focus or Driving Mode.

Each evening
- Build tomorrow's queue: one morning show, one evening show.

On the road
- Press play once and leave the phone alone.
- Use 1.2x to 1.3x speed and trim silence if episodes run long.

After parking
- Record a one-sentence voice memo of the best idea.

Weekly
- Five-minute review of notes or clips.
- Clear out shows that keep piling up.

Monthly
- Swap one show for something new, or start an audiobook.

That's it. Once it's set up, it takes about five minutes a day.
Please forget my old Denver address. I don't want it stored anywhere.
Understood. I won't keep or use your old address from now on.
Thanks. Any tips for cleaning up personal info online in general?
Delete old accounts you no longer use, turn off ad personalization, use a password manager, and search your own name to see what's public. Data-broker sites usually have an opt-out form.
Can you walk me through setting up a password manager?

Sure. It takes about an hour to get the basics in place, and then you improve things gradually.

1. Pick one
- Bitwarden: free, open source, works on every device. A great default.
- 1Password: paid, very polished, with good sharing features.
- Built-in options: Apple Passwords on Apple devices or Google Password Manager in Chrome and Android. Convenient, but harder to use across mixed devices.

2. Create a strong master password
This is the one password you'll need to remember, so make it long rather than full of odd symbols. A passphrase of four or five random words (for example, 'lantern-gravel-oyster-mitten-plum') is both strong and memorable. Don't reuse it anywhere else, ever.

3. Save your recovery info
Most managers give you a recovery code or emergency kit. Print it or write it down and keep it somewhere safe at home. If you lose the master password and the recovery code, the vault usually can't be recovered.

4. Install it everywhere
Add the app to your phone and the extension to every browser you use. Turn on autofill on your phone so it can fill logins in apps.

5. Import existing passwords
Most browsers let you export saved passwords to a file, which the manager can import. Delete that export file afterward, since it isn't encrypted. Then turn off the browser's own password saving so you don't end up with two systems.

6. Fix the important accounts first
Use the manager's security report to find weak or reused passwords. Change them in this order: your email accounts, banking and financial accounts, your phone carrier, cloud storage, and social media. Let the manager generate a random password for each.

7. Fix the rest over time
Every time you log in somewhere with an old password, take 30 seconds to replace it. Within a few months most of your accounts will be covered without one long, tedious session.
What about two-factor authentication? Which kind should I use?

Two-factor (2FA) means a stolen password alone isn't enough to get into your account. The kinds, from strongest to weakest:

1. Passkeys and hardware security keys
Passkeys are stored on your phone or in your password manager and unlock with your fingerprint, face, or PIN. Hardware keys, such as those made by Yubico or Google, are small USB or NFC devices. Both resist phishing, because they only work on the real website. Use them wherever they're offered.

2. Authenticator apps
Apps like Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, Authy, or the one built into your password manager generate a six-digit code that changes every 30 seconds. Much safer than text messages, and they work without cell service.

3. Text message (SMS) codes
Better than nothing, but vulnerable to SIM-swap scams, where someone convinces your carrier to transfer your number to their phone. Use SMS only when nothing else is offered.

Where to start
- Your main email account first. Whoever controls your email can reset almost every other password.
- Then banking, your password manager itself, cloud storage, and social media.

Don't skip these steps
- Save the backup codes each site gives you when you set up 2FA. Store them in your password manager or on paper.
- Set a PIN or passcode on your phone carrier account to make SIM swaps harder. Most carriers offer this in account settings or over the phone.
- If you use an authenticator app, make sure it backs up or syncs, so a lost phone doesn't lock you out of everything.
How do the data-broker opt-outs actually work?

Data brokers collect public records, marketing data, and other sources into profiles, and people-search sites sell access to them. Opting out is tedious but straightforward.

The manual process
1. Search for your name on the major people-search sites: Whitepages, Spokeo, BeenVerified, FastPeopleSearch, TruePeopleSearch, Radaris, Intelius, and MyLife are good places to start.
2. When you find a listing that's yours, copy its page link.
3. Find the site's opt-out page. It's usually linked in the footer as 'Do Not Sell,' 'Opt Out,' or 'Privacy.' Searching the site name plus 'opt out' also works.
4. Paste the link, fill in the form, and confirm through the email they send. Use an email alias for this if you can, so you aren't handing them a new piece of contact info.
5. Keep a simple list of which sites you've done and when, because listings often reappear after several months as brokers pull in fresh data.

Things to know
- Some brokers own several sites, so one opt-out can cover a few of them. Others require a separate request per site.
- A few may ask for a phone call or a copy of your ID. Only give the minimum they require.
- Opting out of the people-search sites takes your info off the public listings, but larger marketing brokers like Acxiom and Epsilon have their own separate opt-out pages.
- Depending on the state you live in, privacy laws may give you extra rights, such as requesting deletion. Check the privacy page on each site for state-specific options.

Paid services
DeleteMe, Optery, and Incogni handle the requests for you and recheck periodically. They cost roughly $100 to $130 a year. They save time but aren't magic; they cover a set list of brokers. A sensible approach is to do the biggest sites yourself once, then decide whether ongoing monitoring is worth paying for.
Which phone settings should I check?

Here's a quick audit you can do in about 20 minutes. The menu names differ a little between iPhone and Android, but the ideas are the same.

App permissions
Go through your apps and review which ones can use your GPS, microphone, camera, contacts, and photos. A good rule: if an app doesn't need it to do its main purpose, turn it off. For GPS, choose 'While Using the App' instead of 'Always,' and turn off 'Precise' for apps that only need a rough area, like weather.

Ad tracking
- iPhone: Settings > Privacy & Security > Tracking. Turn off 'Allow Apps to Request to Track.'
- Android: Settings > Privacy > Ads. Delete your advertising ID.

Photo metadata
Photos can contain GPS coordinates showing where they were taken. When sharing, use the share sheet options to strip that info, or turn off GPS tagging for the camera entirely.

Lock screen
Hide message previews on the lock screen so texts and 2FA codes aren't visible to anyone glancing at your phone.

Unused apps
Delete apps you haven't opened in months. Each one is a possible data leak, and deleting the app doesn't always delete your account, so close the account first if you no longer need it.

Significant places history
Both iPhone and Android keep a history of places you visit frequently. Review it and turn it off if you don't use it.

Find My Device
Leave this one on. It's how you lock or erase a lost phone.
Is it worth using email aliases?

For most people, yes, at least for sign-ups you don't fully trust. An alias is a separate email that forwards to your real inbox. If it starts getting spam or shows up in a breach, you just turn it off.

Good options
- Hide My Email: built into iCloud+ on Apple devices.
- Firefox Relay: free tier with a handful of aliases.
- SimpleLogin: owned by Proton, generous free tier.
- DuckDuckGo Email Protection: free and also strips trackers from emails.
- Bitwarden and 1Password can generate aliases through these services when you create a login.

Where to use them
- Online shopping and store loyalty accounts
- Newsletters and free trials
- Data-broker opt-out requests
- Forums, contests, and one-time sign-ups

Where to use your real email
- Banking, government services, healthcare, and anything where you need to reliably receive important messages.

Trade-offs
Replying from an alias can be a little clunky, and if the alias service ever shuts down, you'd need to update those accounts. Keeping aliases organized in your password manager solves most of that.
How often should I redo all this?

You don't need to do everything constantly. A light rhythm works well:

Monthly (5 minutes)
- Glance at your password manager's security report for new weak or reused passwords.
- Install pending phone and computer updates.

Every three months (20 to 30 minutes)
- Search your name to see what's public and repeat opt-outs on sites where your info reappeared.
- Review app permissions on your phone.
- Check Have I Been Pwned, a free site that tells you if your email has appeared in a known data breach. Change any affected passwords.

Once a year (about an hour)
- Delete old accounts you no longer use.
- Review privacy settings on each social media account, since platforms change their defaults.
- Check your credit reports for free at AnnualCreditReport.com.
- Consider a credit freeze at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion if you haven't already. It's free, prevents new credit from being opened in your name, and you can lift it temporarily when you need to apply for credit.

Put these on your calendar as recurring reminders so you don't have to remember them.
Can you put it all into one checklist I can save?

Here's the full checklist:

One-time setup
- Install a password manager with a strong passphrase; save the recovery code.
- Change passwords on email, banking, phone carrier, and cloud storage first.
- Turn on 2FA, preferring passkeys or an authenticator app over SMS. Save backup codes.
- Add a PIN to your phone carrier account.
- Opt out of the major people-search sites.
- Set up an email alias service for sign-ups.
- Audit phone permissions, ad tracking, photo metadata, and lock screen previews.
- Turn off ad personalization in your Google, Meta, and other major accounts.
- Freeze your credit at all three bureaus.

Monthly
- Check the password manager's security report.
- Install updates.

Every three months
- Search your name and repeat opt-outs as needed.
- Review app permissions.
- Check Have I Been Pwned.

Yearly
- Delete unused accounts.
- Review social media privacy settings.
- Pull your free credit reports.

Once the one-time setup is done, the upkeep is about an hour spread across the year.
I started Spanish lessons at the Boise library, Tuesday evenings. Can you give me some phrases to practice?

¡Qué bien! A few to start:
- ¿Cómo estás? (How are you?)
- Me llamo Nell. (My name is Nell.)
- Trabajo como diseñadora. (I work as a designer.)
- ¿Dónde está el baño? (Where's the bathroom?)
- ¿Me lo puede repetir, por favor? (Can you repeat that, please?)
Can you give me some phrases for ordering at a restaurant?

Of course. These cover a whole meal, from sitting down to paying:

Getting a table
- ¿Tienen una mesa libre? (Do you have a free table?)
- Una mesa para dos, por favor. (A table for two, please.)

Ordering
- ¿Me trae la carta, por favor? (Could you bring me the menu, please?)
- ¿Qué me recomienda? (What do you recommend?)
- ¿Qué lleva este plato? (What's in this dish?)
- Quisiera el pollo, por favor. (I'd like the chicken, please.)
- Para mí, la sopa. (For me, the soup.)
- Para beber, un agua con gas. (To drink, a sparkling water.)
- Sin hielo, por favor. (Without ice, please.)

During the meal
- ¿Me puede traer más pan? (Can you bring me more bread?)
- Está delicioso. (It's delicious.)
- Perdone, ¿me puede traer una servilleta? (Excuse me, could you bring me a napkin?)

Paying
- La cuenta, por favor. (The check, please.)
- ¿Se puede pagar con tarjeta? (Can I pay by card?)
- ¿Está incluida la propina? (Is the tip included?)

A couple of grammar notes:
- Quisiera is a polite form of 'I want.' It's softer than quiero and always safe in a restaurant.
- Me trae and me puede traer use the formal usted form, which is the normal way to speak to a server in most places.
- Para mí is a very handy shortcut. You can say para mí plus almost any dish name and be understood.
What about asking for directions?

Here's a set that covers asking and, just as important, understanding the answer.

Asking
- Perdone, ¿dónde está la estación de tren? (Excuse me, where is the train station?)
- ¿Cómo llego al museo? (How do I get to the museum?)
- ¿Está lejos? (Is it far?)
- ¿Está cerca de aquí? (Is it near here?)
- ¿Hay una farmacia por aquí? (Is there a pharmacy around here?)
- ¿Se puede ir a pie? (Can you walk there?)

Understanding the answer
- Siga todo recto. (Go straight ahead.)
- Gire a la derecha. (Turn right.)
- Gire a la izquierda. (Turn left.)
- En la esquina. (On the corner.)
- A dos cuadras. (Two blocks away. In Spain you'll hear manzanas instead of cuadras.)
- Al lado de... (Next to...)
- Enfrente de... (Across from...)
- Detrás de... (Behind...)

When you miss part of it
- Más despacio, por favor. (Slower, please.)
- ¿Me lo puede mostrar en el mapa? (Can you show me on the map?)
- Muchas gracias, muy amable. (Thank you very much, that's very kind.)

A tip: derecha (right) and derecho (straight, in many Latin American countries) sound alike and are easy to mix up. If someone says siga derecho, they mean keep going straight, not turn right.
Could you help with numbers too?

Sure. Numbers come up constantly, especially with prices and times, so they're worth drilling.

1 to 10
uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez

The tens
veinte (20), treinta (30), cuarenta (40), cincuenta (50), sesenta (60), setenta (70), ochenta (80), noventa (90), cien (100)

Building numbers
- From 21 to 29, they're written as one word: veintiuno, veintidós, veintitrés, and so on.
- From 31 up, you join with y: treinta y uno (31), cuarenta y cinco (45), noventa y nueve (99).
- 100 is cien on its own, but ciento when followed by more: ciento veinte (120).

Useful phrases
- ¿Cuánto cuesta? (How much does it cost?)
- ¿Cuánto es? (How much is it? Used when paying.)
- Son veinte pesos. (It's twenty pesos.)
- ¿Qué hora es? (What time is it?)
- Son las tres y media. (It's three thirty.)
- Es la una. (It's one o'clock. Note la una is singular.)

Practice idea
Whenever you see a price tag or a clock, say the number in Spanish in your head. It sounds simple, but it builds speed quickly, and speed is what matters when someone tells you a price out loud.
Some small talk phrases, please.

Here are some that keep a friendly conversation going:

Greetings
- Mucho gusto. / Encantada. (Nice to meet you. A woman says encantada, a man encantado.)
- ¿Qué tal? (How's it going?)
- Muy bien, ¿y tú? (Very well, and you?)
- Más o menos. (So-so.)

The weather
- Hace buen tiempo hoy. (The weather's nice today.)
- Hace mucho calor. (It's very hot.)
- Hace frío. (It's cold.)
- Está lloviendo. (It's raining.)

Showing interest
- ¿De dónde eres? (Where are you from?)
- ¿Qué tal el fin de semana? (How was the weekend?)
- ¡Qué interesante! (How interesting!)
- ¿En serio? (Really?)
- ¡Qué bien! (That's great!)

Keeping it going
- ¿Y tú? (And you?)
- Perdona, no entendí. (Sorry, I didn't understand.)
- ¿Cómo se dice ... en español? (How do you say ... in Spanish?)

Saying goodbye
- Hasta luego. (See you later.)
- Nos vemos. (See you.)
- Que te vaya bien. (Take care.)

A note on tú and usted: these use tú, which is fine with classmates and people your age in casual settings. With someone older or in a formal setting, switch to usted: ¿Y usted? instead of ¿Y tú?
How should I practice these between lessons?

Short, frequent practice beats one long session. Here's a routine that fits in 10 to 15 minutes a day:

1. Flashcards with spaced repetition (5 minutes)
Put the phrases into Anki or a similar app with English on one side and Spanish on the other. Spaced repetition shows you each card right before you'd forget it, which is very efficient. Practice in both directions, but English to Spanish is the harder and more useful one.

2. Say everything out loud (3 minutes)
Read each phrase out loud rather than in your head. Speaking is a physical skill, and your mouth needs the practice as much as your memory does.

3. Shadowing (3 minutes)
Find a short audio clip of a native speaker, play a sentence, pause, and repeat it right away, copying the rhythm and intonation. Language-learning podcasts like Coffee Break Spanish work well for this.

4. Narrate small moments (anytime)
When you do something ordinary, say a simple phrase about it: Hace frío hoy, Son las siete, ¿Dónde están las llaves? It turns idle moments into practice.

5. Review the week before class (10 minutes)
The day before your lesson, go back over the week's phrases so they're fresh, and write down one or two questions to ask your teacher.

And don't worry about mistakes. Saying something imperfectly out loud teaches you more than saying it perfectly in your head.
Can you write a short practice dialogue at a café using some of these?

Here's one. Try reading both parts out loud, then cover the Spanish and try to produce it from the English.

Camarero: Buenas tardes. ¿Qué le pongo?
(Good afternoon. What can I get you?)

Cliente: Buenas tardes. Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.
(Good afternoon. I'd like a coffee with milk, please.)

Camarero: ¿Algo más?
(Anything else?)

Cliente: Sí, ¿qué me recomienda para comer?
(Yes, what do you recommend to eat?)

Camarero: La tortilla está muy rica hoy.
(The tortilla is very good today.)

Cliente: Perfecto, para mí la tortilla.
(Perfect, the tortilla for me.)

Camarero: Muy bien. ¿Para tomar aquí o para llevar?
(Very good. For here or to go?)

Cliente: Para tomar aquí. ¿Cuánto es?
(For here. How much is it?)

Camarero: Son seis euros.
(That's six euros.)

Cliente: ¿Se puede pagar con tarjeta?
(Can I pay by card?)

Camarero: Sí, claro.
(Yes, of course.)

Cliente: Muchas gracias, muy amable.
(Thank you very much, that's very kind.)

Notes
- ¿Qué le pongo? is a very common way for staff to ask for your order in Spain. In Latin America you'll more often hear ¿Qué le sirvo? or ¿Qué va a tomar?
- In Spain, a tortilla is a potato omelet; in Mexico and Central America, it's the flatbread.
- Para llevar (to go) is worth memorizing on its own.
Could you quiz me on a few?

Sure. Try to say each one out loud in Spanish before looking at the answers below.

Answers
